DESIGNATION OF JUNE 7 AS FAMILY DAY
speechtext:
May I be permitted to make a short announcement. Hon. members may be aware that the Canadian conference on the family, which is sponsored by His Excellency the Governor General and Madame Vanier, will meet in Ottawa from June 7 to June 10. It is the intention of the Governor General to invite the heads of religious denominations in Canada to attend and participate in a special religious observance as part of the opening ceremonies of the conference, to be held on the grounds of Government House on Sunday, June 7.
In recognition of this significant meeting, June 7, 1964 is being designated by the government as "family day". I am sure that all members of this house, and indeed all Canadians, will join with me in wishing the conference every success and in paying this tribute to the important unit in our society, the family.

speechtext:
Last year, Mr. Speaker, my predecessor, the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) decided, as a preliminary study for a redefinition of official policy concerning broadcasting, to ask three persons, that is, the chairman of the board of broadcast governors, Mr. Andrew Stewart, the president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, Alphonse Ouimet, and the president of the association of broadcasters, Mr. Don Jamieson, to examine, from their personal point of view, what is the Canadian policy on broadcasting at the present time and to indicate the points on which they agreed and the aspects on which they could not agree.
These gentlemen, who have now completed their study, have given me a joint report as well as three individual reports. I am ready to table copies of those reports, with the permission of the house.

While the work done by the so-called "troika" will certainly prove to be most useful, the reports show quite clearly that there are still important areas of disagreement. Because of this situation, because of the complicated and urgent issues raised by Canadian broadcasting today, and in order to end present uncertainties, it has been decided to establish a committee on broadcasting whose terms of reference will be as follows: To study, in the light of present and possible future conditions, the purposes and provisions of the Broadcasting Act and related statutes and to recommend what amendments, if any, should be made to the legislation; including an appraisal of the studies being made by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation of its structural organization; and including an inquiry into the financ-

ing of the C.B.C., into C.B.C. consolidation projects, into the relationship between the government and the C.B.C. in so far as the administration and the financing of the corporation are concerned, into the international service of the C.B.C., and into the various means of providing alternative television services, excluding community antenna television systems; and to report their findings to the Secretary of State with their recommendations.
During the course of its study it is expected that the committee will carefully consider the four reports which I am tabling today, and that it will maintain close contact with Dr. Andrew Stewart, Mr. Alphonse Ouimet and Mr. Don Jamieson, who have acquired a long and valuable experience in the field of broadcasting.
The committee will be comprised of three members, as follows: Mr. Robert Fowler, Mr. Marc Lalonde, Mr. Ernest Steele. This will be an advisory committee to the Secretary of State. It will proceed with its important work as quickly as possible in order to present its report and recommendations at the beginning of 1965. When the report has been received and made public, the government intends to introduce appropriate new legislation and to refer that legislation to a parliamentary committee for detailed study and consideration.
The advisory committee will not study th'e subject of community antenna television systems. The B.B.G. and the Department of Transport have already made such a study and on March 19 made joint recommendations to the government, which hopes to make known its policy on cable television within a short time.

I did not take that out of the minister's announcement because I felt that it was only there he was being specific. If we are going to consider the purpose of the act, and recommend amendments to the act, it would seem to me that the review must touch private broadcasting stations and the whole picture of their relationships.
We certainly feel that the three people chosen, most of whom are well known by members, are able and fair and capable of doing an excellent job. We feel that the exclusion of C.A.T.V. from the committee study is a very wise move. It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, from the controversy that is developing in the United States, where you have the broadcasting networks and the C.A.T.V. people joining in a monster national battle, that a decision will have to come very soon to determine the community antenna television problem; otherwise it may be too late and we will have a really disastrous problem on our hands.

speechtext:
What action, in detail, has been taken with respect to each of the following recommendations of the Joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on Indian affairs:
Questions
"(a) The act should provide for a term of office for band councils of not more than three years with one third of the members elected each year.
(b)	All band members, who are otherwise qualified, should be allowed to vote at band elections and on any other matter affecting the band if present on the reserve when the election is held.
(c)	The chief should be elected by the band members rather than from the elected council.
(d)	An oath of office for band council members should be required.
(e)	The Indian Act should set out specific duties and authorities of the chief.
(f)	The act should provide for filling a vacancy in a band council as soon as possible after the vacancy occurs.
(g)	There should be an extensive educational program to acquaint band councils with the Indian Act and regulations and with council authority.
(h)	It should be the definite policy of government to move toward more self governing bands and to this end more bands should be given control of their revenue funds.
(i)	There should be a decrease in ministerial and governmental authority with a concomitant increase in band council authority.
(j)	Bylaw authority under the act should be combined and additional powers granted.
(k)	To assist elected band councils in local self government, per capita grants on an unconditional basis should be made."?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT INDIAN AFFAIRS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
(a), (b), (d), (e), (i), (j) and (k). These recommendations would require legislation to implement with relevant changes in existing provisions of the Indian Act. A review of the Indian Act is proceeding as quickly as sound and thorough consideration will permit with the objective of submitting appropriate amendments.
(c) To restrict the election of a chief to a majority vote of the electors would require changes in the Indian Act, as it now provides under section 73(3) for the election of the chief by a majority vote of the electors, or by a vote of the elected councillors from among themselves.
(f)	In accordance with the provisions of section 77(4) of the Indian Act, a special election may be held to fill a vacancy when such vacancy occurs in a band council more than three months before the date when another election would ordinarily be held. The general practice is to hold such special elections in consultation with the band council concerned.
(g)	The development of Indian leadership is carried on with the co-operation and assistance of provincial governments and university extension departments. Sixteen leadership training courses were held in 1963-64. These were attended by chiefs and councillors and other real and potential leaders on the reserves.
The purpose of these courses was to train those who attended in order that they might increase their competence in the field of leadership in reserve activities. Although the content of the courses varied depending on the wishes of the trainees, subjects covered

Questions
were frequently concerned with recognizing problems, planning and taking action to solve these problems, methods of communication, public speaking, understanding the community and its economic and human resources, knowledge of Indian affairs branch administration and existing programs, federal, provincial, and local resources that are available and how to obtain this assistance when required.
(h)	The department is already moving ahead in this field. Progress is dependant upon the readiness and ability of Indian bands to assume the additional authority and responsibility which may be conferred under the Indian Act. Since 1959, 76 bands have been granted permission to control, manage and expend in whole or in part their revenue moneys.

subtopic: CONFERENCE ON FORESTRY INSECTS AND DISEASES
CONFERENCE ON FORESTRY INSECTS AND DISEASES
speechtext:
1.	Will government specialists in forest entomology and pathology participate in the seminar on insects and diseases harmful to forests, to be held in England from July 20 to July 30 and, if so, what are the names of the specialists, what work does each do for the department, and who will lead the delegation?
2.	What contribution will Canada make to this conference?
3.	Is Canada a member of the international union of forestry research organizations and, if so (a) since what date (b) how much does such membership cost this country (c) what have been the main Canadian contributions to this organization?
4.	In the Department of Forestry, who is responsible for Canadian participation in this organization?

Answer: 1. Yes. The following specialists employed by the federal government will take part in the seminar on insects and diseases harmful to forests, which will take place in England in 1964:
B. M. McGugan, associate director (entomology), forest entomology and pathology branch, Ottawa; V. J. Nordin, director (pathology), forest entomology and pathology branch, Ottawa; R. M. Belyea, chief of forest entomology and pathology laboratory, Fredericton; R. Pomerleau, chief of forest pathology research, forest entomology and pathology laboratory, Quebec; L. T. White, chief, forest pathology laboratory, Maple (Ontario); W. A. Reeks, chief, forest insect laboratory, Sault Ste. Marie (Ontario); F. E. Webb, chief, forest entomology laboratory, Winnipeg; G. P. Thomas, chief, forest entomology and pathology laboratory, Calgary; R. R. Lejeune, chief, forest entomology and pathology laboratory, Victoria.
The delegation is under the joint direction of Mr. McGugan, in charge of the entomological personnel, and Mr. Nordin, in charge of the pathological personnel.
2.	The delegates of the forestry department will take part in the general discussions on the threat caused by the intercontinental dissemination of forest insects, and tree diseases, as well as on the means of lessening that threat, and they also have written the various briefs listed hereafter:
Repercussions of Tree Diseases on Forest Production in North America; Intercontinental Spreading of Forest Pathogenic Agents; Possible Dangers Resulting from Root Diseases; Forest Entomology in Canada; The Role of the Forest Entomologist.
3.	The Canadian members of the international union of forestry research organizations include the forestry departments of several Canadian universities, the Minister of Forestry and some other research organizations. (a) The forestry service of the former
Questions
department of the interior became a member of the international union of forestry-research organizations in 1932. (b) The yearly fee is $30. (c) The main contributions of the Department of Forestry to this organization include its representation in the standing committee, the participation of officers of the department in the studies of technical sections dealing with various aspects of forest management, for instance, fires, soils and forestry types, tree diseases, insects and forest products, as well as the presence of its delegates to the meetings of the congresses which are held periodically every three or five years.
4.	The participation of the forestry department in the studies of the international union of forestry research organizations is the responsibility of the deputy minister of forestry, as well as that of the directors of the three research branches of the department he may delegate.

LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is the 25th of May. Like many other Canadians I took the opportunity last week end to travel through parts of our country at this most beautiful time of the year. To my sorrow I find that the country is dividing on the subject of the flag. At a time when all our hopes should be centred upon uniting the country, this matter is now becoming a partisan issue and one, I am afraid, of a deeply emotional character.
This effort on the part of the government to force a shotgun decision on the people of Canada causes us to wonder why. I am going to suggest that one of the reasons for their great haste and the manner in which they are carrying forward this project is that they are desirous of covering up a whole series of sins of omission.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: And commission.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
People are wondering if this is not a device on the part of the government for the purpose not only of hiding the long list of promises unfulfilled, not only to cover up their sins of omission, but also to whitewash their sins of commission or to draw a red herring across the trail. They are wondering whether there is an election coming and, if it is coming sooner than parliament desires, if it is simply because a budget will have to be brought down at the next session of parliament which will involve all sorts of new taxes that will be required to get the government out of its present difficulties.
The subject of the flag is one on which we should all be tending to unite on the basis of a common pride and love not only for the beauty of our country but for those things for which we have stood and fought over the years, but we know that you cannot build up pride in any flag unless there is a record of achievement under that flag. We know that in Canada today discrimination of an economic sort exists. Whether it be among workers in factories of our great cities, people trying to build homes in the suburbs around our great cities or even farmers, as long as discrimination exists you cannot have a strong Canada and there is very little use in talking about a

flag around which we can all unite. We cannot talk about rallying the people of this nation in pride around a flag as long as this discrimination exists.
I am going to bring to light something that is not new. It is one of the sins of omission of the government which I believe they are trying to hide with all the emotional discussion about a flag. They are trying to divide Canada to hide the fact that no action has been taken with regard to this particular sin of omission.
The government has been in power for over a year. During that year we have had 60 days of decision and 300 days of retreating. We are wondering where the retreating is going to stop. We would like to see the government not try to hide these vital economic issues by dividing the country on an emotional issue such as the symbol of our sovereignty. We want the government to get on with the job of correcting these economic discriminations.
As one member of the opposition I have tried on several occasions to bring to the attention of the people of Canada the fact that discrimination does exist between the farmers in the better farming areas who have markets for their products and the farmers in other areas which are not so good and who do not have markets. Several times I have brought this matter forward in the house on behalf of the party of which I am a member. Several times other members have supported the points of view I have expressed, yet no action has been taken.
I would recall to the house that on October 14, 1963, I took advantage of the democratic opportunity provided by the rules of the house to move an amendment to a supply motion which dealt with the plight of eastern farmers. I placed on the record at that timetables of statistics from the dominion bureau of statistics and the department concerned to show the level to which a large percentage of the farmers in eastern Canada had fallen. I also included the farmers of British Columbia in my remarks at that time.
Yet on May 25, 1964, I once again have to take advantage of the democratic opportunity provided on a motion for supply under our rules to bring forward matters about which the government has done nothing, in order to direct the attention of the people of Canada once more to the matter of action to assist the eastern farmers. There is much reason to be more satisfied today that this problem is being paid more attention by the public than was the case a year or two ago. Many newspapers are beginning to recognize that as the wealth of the farming community goes, so goes the wealth of the whole nation.

As recently as today that august newspaper the Montreal Gazette tells us how the great sales of wheat to the nations of the world have begun to lift up the economy of Canada and cause it to move forward even faster than before. These great sales of wheat are not enough, Mr. Speaker, unless they are backed by a program that will deal with the trouble spots. All the Liberals can say is, what did you do when you were in power? Once again I should like them to listen to the answer.
After we took power in 1957, following a generation of inactivity by the previous government, we announced a national agriculture program in this house in August, 1958. We systematically tried to carry out that program, and with some success. It was clear that the program was working for those farmers whose operations were of a commercial character, that is farmers who could take advantage of the various pieces of legislation and regulations that we had introduced to build up their economic life. It was also easily apparent that those pieces of legislation, those various acts of the government, were not sufficient to help the farmer at the bottom of the totem pole. We introduced, therefore, the well known piece of legislation called ARDA, the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act. This was a long range program and had to be backed up by a series of regional, short range programs to get at the pressing problems of the areas in agriculture which were not doing well. These areas in agriculture could be found by calculating the income of the farmers.
On October 14 of last year, therefore, I put on the record of the house a series of figures to illustrate where I thought the problem was most serious. At that time I pointed out that we had gone to the country in 1962 and again in 1963 with a program to meet those conditions. We had worked out as a government, I say with some satisfaction, a program which was received well in the rural areas of B.C., the rural areas of the west, the rural areas of Ontario, and yes, even in the rural areas of Quebec and the maritimes, as the number of members here from rural areas indicates. This was a program that received no particular publicity in the city areas. However, it was a sound Canadian program because we realized we could not ever build a strong Canada if some segments of the population were weak.
We were right in 1957 and 1958 in saying that agriculture had to be built up. We attempted to do so. I think we succeeded. But there is no use being complacent about success if some segments of the agricultural
Eastern Agricultural Assistance population do not share equally in the benefits others are receiving. So on October 14, 1963, I gave the country an opportunity of seeing some of the statistics, and how awful they were.
This battle is slowly being lost because of the fact that we have, as an agency of government, the dominion bureau of statistics. I have in my hand a bulletin issued last Friday, May 22, and it illustrates the reason we are losing the battle. I tried to inform Canadians that there was a problem and that you cannot build a strong Canada if some people remain weak. Listen to this statement which was issued last Friday:
Farm cash income from farming operations, excluding supplementary payments, in Canada (excluding Newfoundland) was estimated at an alltime high of $3,219.1 million in 1963, up by 2.1 per cent from 1962's preceding peak of $3,154.2 million. Higher receipts from the sale of wheat, coarse grain, tobacco, and poultry and dairy products contributed most to the increase.
This is the type of statement that is detrimental to the efforts we are making in this house to bring to the attention of Canadians a situation which is not good for the people of this country. If you go on and read the advance statement for the whole year, which was compiled by the dominion bureau of statistics, you will find they amended these figures to show that the income was up 2.1 per cent. They say that farm income is up 2.2 per cent. How can you blame the people who write our newspaper articles, who are the medium for education of our people in Canada, when they see this type of statement?
At this point I should like to go back and read the statement the minister made in introducing his estimates in this house on April 24, I believe, just about a month ago. He repeated this statement and held it up to the people of Canada as evidence that everything was well in agriculture. Everything is not well in agriculture, Mr. Speaker. What I want to do now is find out where the truth lies so that hon. members in the house will know. Let those who disseminate information disseminate the truth and not this type of meaningless claptrap.
What is the truth? Let me quote some figures that I think make sense. First of all, the Ethiopian in the woodpile in so far as these figures are concerned is the fact that they refer to net income. Net income is meaningless. It is the silliest sort of thing you ever saw, and I will illustrate that statement by dealing with the figures for the province of Saskatchewan. The net income for the province of Saskatchewan for 1961 is stated as $132 million. In 1962 the net income for the province of Saskatchewan in agriculture is stated as $506 million. Therefore from the

Eastern Agricultural Assistance year 1961 to the year 1962, farm net income, according to the dominion bureau of statistics, went up nearly four times. Nothing could be more asinine than a statement like that. In 1961 you have all the editors crying how poor the farmer in Saskatchewan is, that all he made was $132 million. In 1962 they said he made $506 million, almost four times as much, so look how wealthy the farmer is. Then everybody gets mad at him.
These figures do not tell the story, Mr. Speaker. If you go on to 1963, the last figures we have, we find the net income for Saskatchewan is shown as $603 million. Everybody says, isn't the farmer doing well? He made $506 million in 1962 and $603 million in 1963, compared with $132 million back in 1961, only two years earlier. These figures do not tell the true story, because it has been assumed that the people who read these statements are knowledgeable as to how the figures are put together, and this is not true.
I should like to put on the record, if I may, the real figures for income for Saskatchewan in those years. In 1961 the realized net income, that is the cash that goes into the farmer's pocket-and that is the only thing that means anything-was not $132 million but was $343 million. These statements that were conceived in the city of Ottawa were out by over $200 million in the case of one province alone. In the year 1962, instead of $506 million, when everybody thought the Saskatchewan farmer was wealthy, the net income was $413 million. The increased income was nothing like $506 million. In 1963, when the published statement showed the net income as $603 million, the farmers' real income was down some $43 million to $370 million. I am glad the Minister of Trade and Commerce is sitting in his seat today because he knows why the income was down last year. He knows 1962 was a good year. He knows 1963 was an even better year.
Why did the farm net income in Saskatchewan go down by $43 million last year, the best year in our history? He knows that last year he would not listen when I, on behalf of the official opposition, proposed that he take certain steps to see that grain could be moved out of the St. Lawrence efficiently. He stated he knew how to move grain; he had been deputy minister under Mr. Howe. What happened? We lost days of shipping time out of the St. Lawrence because of his failure to act. Later on I felt the shipping situation in British Columbia was going bad. He said something would be done and it would be done his way, not my way. He knows that as a result they had to turn down orders for grain through the west coast ports 

last fall. The businessmen out there showed what they could do when you went out there and challenged them. They shipped 29 million bushels in one month. This drop in farm income was due entirely to this matter of not getting the grain out of the country. So the farmers' income was down this $43 million.
I am not worrying about the Saskatchewan farmer; he knows he will get the money eventually. I am simply pointing out that on these figures of net income, which make such beautiful and wonderful headlines, they tell the city people that the Saskatchewan farmers got up to $603 million in 1963 whereas their real income was not $603 million but about $370 million, just about half.
I would like to explain how you get this difference between realized and net income. People in the d.b.s. who keep these figures are sound statisticians. They are good bookkeepers, and when a farmer earns so much money they call that gross cash income. They take off his operating and depreciation costs and then they get his realized net income, the money in his pocket. They have another figure called inventory, and when a farmer grows a big crop or raises a lot of cattle and does not sell them they add the value to his income, and according to these figures he is very wealthy yet he has not got any money in his pocket.
The next year, when the farmer sells all that surplus, since they added it on to his income the previous year they take it off this year from the money in his pocket. Therefore net income is a meaningless figure, and is only for experts in the back room. I would plead with those who disseminate information in this country to keep away from giving the net income figure. It brings bad feelings between the city and the country, and it does not give a true picture of farm income. What you want to disseminate is the money in the farmers' pocket, and that will tell the story.
Let me tell the grim story of agriculture during the last year or so. I have in my hand figures of the realized net income, in millions of dollars, as issued by the d.b.s., which stated that net farm income was up 2.2 per cent across Canada last year or, according to the revised figures in the last bulletin, up 2.1 per cent. Whether it is 2.2 per cent or 2.1 per cent, it is a fact that there was a decrease in realized net income in every province of Canada, except two, in 1963.
Let me give the figures. In Prince Edward Island in 1958 realized income was $12,579 million, and in 1963 it was down to $6,908 million. I would not want to say it is down by half, but it is getting very close to half

what it was a few years ago. This decrease has been going on every year and continued in 1963.
In Nova Scotia in 1958 realized farm income was $15,898 million and in 1963 it was down to $11,161 million. In 1962 it was down to $13,557 million, so this shows a decrease of roughly $5 million in a seven year period. In percentages, it is almost a third.
Surely there must be some New Brunswick members in the house who would be interested in knowing that realized farm income in New Brunswick last year was $12,188 million, in 1962 it was $12,840 million, and seven years ago, in 1958, it was $21,218 million. It is now down to almost half what it was in 1958. Surely this means something to somebody.
In Quebec the situation is static, because the good farmers of Quebec are building up their income while the other 40 per cent or 50 per cent, who are on poor farms, are going steadily downhill, which means that the net result is almost static. In 1958 Quebec realized farm income was $196,645,000 and it dropped to $189,822,000 in 1963. This is not a matter of satisfaction that the good farmer's income is going up while the poor farmer's is going down.
I wonder how many members of parliament from these provinces will stand up and fight for these areas that are not doing so well. These are not just statistics; these are the stories of farmers I have met and known. These are the stories of my fellow Canadians who have a right not just to have a member of parliament in this house, but to have every member of parliament concerned about discrimination against those who are not doing so well.
I could go through the list of the provinces, but let me just leave this one figure with you; that in all the provinces of Canada, with the exception of two, realized farm income went down last year, and those two provinces do not include Saskatchewan and Alberta. We went down too, but we know why we went down and we will correct that. I give those figures because this is the truth and not this meaningless gibberish that comes from the d.b.s., which is of course satisfactory for bookkeepers but should not be used by people who have not reached the mental status where they can understand these figures.
I have tried in blunt terms to put the realized income figures on the record. I do not like to make speeches which are just tearing down the government all the time. I have been quite blunt about what I think is a failure on the part of the government. These points were all brought out in previous years, 20220-225
Eastern Agricultural Assistance yet all the government can do is reply "What did you do when you were in power"? We, when we were in power, at least brought to the attention of the people how bad the situation was, and we prepared long range programs. We launched the study of those special areas in eastern Canada where the situation was very bad. The report of that study has never been published and should be made public now.
We were the ones who went into the 1962 and 1963 election campaigns with a program for building up eastern agriculture. We were the government which, in the speech from the throne in 1962, brought in a program to meet the situation, and we were the government which was thrown out of office on the nuclear issue on February 5, 1963, before we could bring our new farm program into effect. We were the ones who brought in a program that would take two or three years to implement, but we were thrown out on what I think was a bogus issue. However, the people of Canada will decide these things in due course.
I now hope that this tendency to quote net income figures, which show how wealthy you are when you are not, and how broke you are when you are not, will come to an end. I hope from now on we will be given the realized net income figures. When he looks at these figures province by province what member of parliament from Quebec, whether he sits on the government side or on the opposition side, is happy to sit here looking at those figures for the last few years? What member of parliament from the province of New Brunswick, no matter on which side of the house he sits, is happy about these figures? What member of parliament from Nova Scotia can be happy about these figures? I know these people, and I know that something has to be done.
Just to show how bad the situation is, if I could have permission from the house I would like to table these two sets of figures so that members could study them. Mr. Speaker, can I have permission to table them? One gives the d.b.s. figures on realized net income and the other gives the figures of income distribution, survey of farms in eastern Canada, preliminary data, prepared in the Department of Agriculture.

speechtext:
The second table is from the income distribution survey of farms in eastern Canada, data which was quoted by an official of the Department of Agriculture in 1963, and this table delineates the problem. All I am going to say here is that 43 per cent of the farm families in the eastern part of Canada, that is in the northern and eastern part of Ontario and then on east to Quebec and the Atlantic provinces, have a total income-this is an average figure-of $2,800 or less; and from the tables I put on the record on October 14, 1963, you will see that more than half that income comes from income outside farms. This is total income of $2,800, out of which they have to pay taxes, look after their families and pay farm operating expenses. Of that $2,800, we see that 53 per cent comes from sales of farm produce. This means that 43 per cent of the farmers in the Ottawa valley, the northern part of Ontario, all through Quebec, P.E.I., New Brunswick and Nova Scotia have an average income from their farms, out of which they have to pay all expenses, of roughly $1,400. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that these figures show where the problem lies.
Having made those points, I would like to conclude by suggesting a program for the regions of Canada in which there is this economic discrimination. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that under the national agricultural

program that we laid down in 1958 we proposed a long range program and suggested, in the seventh point, that there should be regional programs to meet regional needs. I am going to list a regional program for eastern Canada to give some direction to the government, not with the idea alone that they should follow these suggestions but to at least give them something they can study. I know they have no ideas of their own at the moment. Their ideas do not show up, at least. Here are the ideas I put forward for their consideration. First, there should be a feed grain policy that stabilizes prices. Second, there should be a fertilizer policy that gets at this job of increasing the income of the low income farmer. Hon. members will see the importance of this by reading from the d.b.s. bulletin of February, 1964 entitled "Farm Net Income, Advanced Statement". It says:
Farm operating expenses and depreciation charges advanced from the revised estimate.. .an increase of slightly less than 5 per cent.
Then it says:
-with the more important increases being recorded for feed, fertilizers and the operation of farm machinery, including repairs.
This means that policies in respect of feed grain and fertilizer should be devised to meet this problem. Feed grain amounts to about 25 per cent of the cost of running an eastern farm, and this is the No. 1 pressing problem.

Fertilizer is growing in importance and this problem should be met head on before the opportunity goes by. With regard to farm machinery, we have heard a great deal from the Minister of Agriculture as to what he is going to do, but there has been no action.
Next is the fourth point. We need some sort of a pasture policy to get increased production off the grass in eastern Canada. Yesterday I was looking at some of these pastures and talking to the farmers about what could be done, and I know there is a very simple way of getting it done. Fifth, we need a water policy for the eastern provinces, something similar to P.F.R.A. and the programs that apply to the west. Then we need a livestock policy for the whole country, with particular reference to the east. Next, as I said when the estimates of the Department of Agriculture were being discussed, there has to be a national dairy policy, because dairy products are now produced and distributed in the whole country-in fact, they even go abroad. We should apply this national dairy policy to the regional problems which exist.
With regard to eastern feed grains, as I said a moment ago this is the No. 1 need. It costs the average eastern farmer 25 per cent of his total expenditures to buy feed grains. Last year when the government made several policy changes in the summer I told them, on behalf of the official opposition, that their policy would not succeed in stabilizing prices. The ordinary person said, "All right; let us wait for a year and see if this policy will stabilize prices". The hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent) started to give the figures when these estimates were under discussion a couple of weeks ago. He will give the figures tomorrow, which will bear out what I have said that these prices were not stabilized and last winter there was a large jump in the last few months of winter feeding.
The standing committee on agriculture and colonization does offer us some hope in this connection and I would suggest to the government very seriously, and I think with some correctness, that if the members on that committee are allowed to act as an allparty committee, the Liberals, the Conservatives, the N.D.P., Social Credit and the Credi-tistes, something can be done in this regard.
I have looked at the composition of that committee and have measured the calibre of the men on it. We could come up with a strong program supported by all parties if the government will let the members of the committee act as members trying to help agriculture in eastern Canada. I know this question relates to the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauv6)
Eastern Agricultural Assistance and not the Minister of Agriculture, because the Minister of Forestry now looks after this question, but if he will give us a policy statement that the members of this committee could work in a non-partisan way, I think they could come up with an answer to these problems.
With regard to the marginal farmer, after the report of January, 1963 I gave some figures to the house on October 14 of that year, and I suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that he should let us have this report. If we have it I think some of us will be able to come forward and make some policy suggestions which will really help solve some of the problems faced by the marginal farmer. In my previous remarks on this subject last year I suggested that action be taken along educational and sociological lines, but we need the full report on this subject so that our policies can be based on fact and be made more effective.
I have almost concluded my remarks, Mr. Speaker, but I wish to wind up by saying that I do not think it is enough for the Liberal members on the other side of the chamber, when I quote these figures of low income in eastern Canada, to stand up and say, "What did you do?" That shows an empty mind and a bankruptcy of ideas. I would ask them to just remember that ARDA gets at the job on a long range basis, and they will only hinder the solution of these problems by the kind of monkeyshines to which I referred in a previous debate. ARDA will point the way a little bit, but something more is necessary. I ask the government to remember that the Conservative party drew up this program to help eastern agriculture. It helped eastern agriculture in 1962 and 1963, and we should be prepared to act upon it now.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, we do not have to draw a diagram for the government. We know they are out of ideas, but we are simply asking them to accept our positive suggestions and begin to move on them. There is no use at all saying that there are going to be amendments to the Farm Credit Corporation Act to double the amount lent from $20,000 to $40,000, and so on. This does not get at the problem of the little farmer. There is no use at all saying there will be amendments to the Crop Insurance Act, because this only helps those provinces where crop insurance is in effect; those are the only farmers who would benefit from these amendments. I ask the government not to tell us they contemplate taking some secret action with regard to farm machinery; I ask them to bring this action forward so we may consider it.

Eastern Agricultural Assistance I am simply saying, Mr. Speaker, that at this moment we should seriously consider this amendment to the resolution to go into committee:
That all the words after "That" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets the continuing failure of the government to take effective action with regard to the pressing agricultural problems of eastern Canada".
I am moving this motion, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska, and I have a copy here in French. While these copies are being distributed I would like to wind up by simply saying that at this time hon. members of the house should, with their vote, make sure that we are not using the flag issue as something to hide the real problems facing Canada today. It will bring more satisfaction to the workers in our cities, as I said earlier, the people in our suburbs, and our farmers, if they know that this house is moving to solve the economic problems that are causing unrest, and is not using matters such as the flag, and other matters, to cover up the real economic problems facing Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I submit that the present amendment should be declared out of order because the matter has already been submitted to the house and passed upon in the form of a previous motion, although the said motion was not worded in exactly the same manner.
May I refer Your Honour to the Votes and Proceedings of this house for Monday, May 4, 1964, page 284, to a motion that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair. The hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), seconded by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming), moved an amendment to that motion in the following terms:
That the motion be amended by striking out all the words after "That" and substituting therefor:
"this house condemns the neglect of the government"-
Then the motion follows, and concludes in this manner:
"And urges the government, in the interests of national development, to take immediate action to make up for the year of neglect of this problem by forthwith:
(1)	establishing a national advisory committee on water resources to assist in co-ordinating national resource development:
(2)	accelerating the application of ARDA policies to the problems of national resource development.
Just in case an attempt might be made to argue that the first amendment put by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris on Monday, May 4 ought to be interpreted as limited to referring to the protection of water resources, I would draw to Your Honour's attention that on the same date a subamendment was 
proposed and that that subamendment dealt squarely and completely with all policies relating to ARDA, and therefore to eastern agriculture. That amendment is to be found at page 285 of Votes and Proceedings and reads as follows:
__"and practical steps in the best interests of
national development to accelerate the application of ARDA policies."
If one refers to Votes and Proceedings for Tuesday, May 5, 1964, one notes first at page 289 that the subamendment to which I have just referred is recorded as having been substantially defeated. Then at page 290 the principal amendment is also reported as having been defeated.
May I repeat for Your Honour the last part of standing order 35 of the rules of this house, which reads as follows:
No member may reflect upon any vote of the house, except for the purpose of moving that such vote be rescinded.
It is a rule of practice in this house that whenever a question has been decided in the course of a session the matter be not put again to the house by way of amendment in the same session. I should like to quote first of all citation 200 (1) of Beauchesne's fourth edition, which is to be found at page 167.
(1) An old rule of parliament reads:	"That
a question being once made and carried in the affirmative or negative, cannot be questioned again but must stand as the judgment of the house." Unless such a rule were in existence, the time of the house might be used in the discussion of motions of the same nature and contradictory decisions would be sometimes arrived at in the course of the same session.
Lastly I should like to quote citation 203 (7) of Beauchesne's fourth edition, which is to be found at page 172:
(7) Mr. Speaker Sproule on the 13th February, 1913, decided that a proposed amendment which was substantially the same motion as the member had moved on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, was not in order because "a motion must not raise a question substantially identical with one on which the house has given a decision in the same session".
For that reason I suggest respectfully that the amendment ought to be declared out of order.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, although I have the greatest respect for the government house leader I must say that I find his argument somewhat tenuous.
