maintopic: REALIZED NET FARM INCOME IN CANADA
speechtext:
I was
very surprised to learn that the amendment today would be on agriculture, because of the auspicious beginning of the statement by the former minister of agriculture dealing with another subject. I was also surprised to learn that the subject matter of the hon. member's speech has been discussed every time the subject of agriculture has been before the house for the past two years. It was a good speech in the beginning and there was a good deal to commend it to the people. But a great deal of the information and philosophy in that

speech have now been accomplished, and I think if anyone intends to move a non-confidence motion he should do it on a much broader scale.
It also strikes me as being very odd to hear someone say he wishes to make a non-political speech and a non-partisan suggestion on the basis of a non-political scheme for the economy-a scheme for agriculturists and farmers across Canada-and then in a partisan way go ahead to move a motion of no confidence. This may fit in with the rest of the speech, and maybe it becomes an amusing matter, but I doubt this because many of us know that the concern felt for agriculture is fairly fundamental across the nation; it does not apply only to eastern agriculture. Although the problems may be more pressing in that area, there is a great similarity between the problems in eastern Canada and those that have been brought to our attention by many of those representing the western farmers.
The concern for agriculture is a continuing one, and one that warrants some consideration. One matter of concern is the operations of the committee on agriculture. Since I have had the honour of being a member of that committee, and it may be a dubious honour on many occasions, the committee has discussed several very important problems. But whether the government of Canada is Conservative or Liberal we find that there is a failure on the part of the government to relate the work done by members of parliament in the committee to actual legislation.
I should like to refer to one such committee of several years ago. We heard briefs from every farm machinery company, every farm organization and from many individuals. Certainly the work done by the committee as a whole and by individual members of the committee should be commended. It was very interesting to hear members of the committee speak about farm machinery prices and point out some of the difficulties on the basis of their own experience. They knew exactly what they were talking about. They knew how to solve the problem and could offer clear and definite suggestions to improve the situation.
But what do we do? The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) gets up and says that this is one of the most pressing problems. Pressing, my foot! If it was pressing why did he not refer it to the committee this year? What has the committee got before it now? The tobacco industry. This is also a very important field, but we spent a year discussing the subject of farm machinery. I have a cabinet full of submissions made by farm organizations, the proceedings of our investigations and studies that were prepared on our behalf. We got
Eastern Agricultural Assistance half way into the matter and then what happened? I do not know what happened, but certainly no government acted on the matter. All the material we gathered has just stayed in the files in the minister's office as it has in mine. If the minister wants to do anything about the matter all he needs to do is to look at his files and he will find there are quite a number of things he can do. He does not need to go to the committee again to ascertain what they are. There are many very simple things that can be done.
We should eliminate the morass of equipment available which cannot be interchanged with other equipment. Every time a new tractor is produced it probably makes obsolete all the equipment that the older tractor drew behind it. It is a very simple thing to make the hydraulic connections the same for all tractors. If necessary we can pass a law saying that they will all be of a specific size and interchangeable. It is not hard to do. The minister wants to help the farmers to save money. This would probably save my brother $1,000 a year because of the equipment he uses on his farm.
I am sure there are many members here who operate farms on a much larger scale where the saving would be much larger. The minister knows this. He has studied this problem. But what do we do about it? Every member of the house who stands up and makes a speech like that made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) is drawing a red herring, like the red flag, across the problems of agriculture. The hon. member did not really make any specific suggestion. What he was doing was drawing a vision.
I could go into all aspects of the farm machinery situation. We listened to the subject being discussed for months. From the farm machinery companies we certainly heard some of the most fantastic financial reports that have come before a committee of the house in many years. If there ever was a free wheeling, international dealing bunch of financiers it is those in the farm implement industry.
What does the minister do about the matter? Does he have to sit in his seat and say he does not understand, that he does not know anything about it? Can he honestly say that he cannot stand up in the house and make even one suggestion that will help to solve some of the problems? We do not need a committee. The problem has been discussed. It would have been nice if we could have gone to Europe and seen what some of the other countries were doing. What did the Conservative government say? They said it could not be done now, that they would have

Eastern Agricultural Assistance to go back to the house and get permission. You know the old story: Put it off till tomorrow; don't worry about the bridge because we may never get there, and it will not matter whether it is up or down.
This situation has been going on for a long time. If we wanted to do something about the farm machinery problem the committee should have been continued. I have not heard the minister stand up in the house and say: Let us get the committee organized immediately. I attended the first meeting of the steering committee the other day. We all know that last year I made a real fuss about calling the committee to meet and that members of the government would not come to the meetings because they did not want the committee to meet. I do not want to have to go through that again. I can be a proper s.o.b. if I have to, but I do not want to have to be all the time. I am quite happy for somebody else to do it. But some of the responsibility falls on the minister. Every farmer in the country knows something about the problem.
There is another thing that is very simple. In the defence committee we decided that there would be standardization of nut and bolt sizes. So far as the farmers are concerned, if this were done the farmer would know he would get the right size when he sent to town for half a dozen bolts to fix his plow. They would be standardized. Now there are many different sizes being used. Many of these things will save the farmer a hundred dollars a year.
The former minister went on to talk about other problems. One he named was feed grain. What did we do about feed grain? The committee sat and received a very good education in the matter. I have learned a lot about agriculture and the wheat deal. I always said that the wheat board made the deal. The former minister said that he had made the wheat deal with China. I find out that he is wrong, too. The people who made the deal were people we did not know existed. The free wheeling grain brokers of this country were the people who made the wheat deal.
We found out quite a bit about feed grain. We got quite an education. But surely I was not elected just to be educated, Mr. Speaker. Once we have the knowledge surely we should be able to make legislative decisions on these matters. But what did we do? The minister did not even ask that the matter of feed grain be referred again to the committee so they could solve the problem of the eastern farmers in this regard. Instead, the subject of tobacco was referred to the committee. This came about because somebody in-


troduced a very dangerous, political resolution on the tobacco problem. It was referred to the committee because otherwise it might have been voted on in the house and something might have actually had to be done about it. What a red herring that turned out to be.
I am not saying that the tobacco problem is not important. It is important, but surely we should settle one problem before we jump into something else. Let us not play around with things and use them as red herrings. Is the committee simply a rug under which to sweep everything? Are we to discuss a matter for a little while and then take up a new problem and sweep the other one under the rug? The problem of feed grain could have been solved.
I have reports from farmers in this area that are in conflict with the statements we received with regard to the grain that was being held in this area for consumption on the farms last winter. I find that in the Arnprior area the price went up $7 or $8. This should not have happened, of course, because the grain was already in storage in the great lakes area or at Prescott. The minister had made provision for the storage costs so there would be no increase in the price of grain during the year. Yet the price went up $7 or $8. My colleague says that parliament did it. Parliament can only act when the minister brings matters before us. In my opinion this is where he fails all the time. He does not bring the right things before parliament. If he would give us the opportunity to do something about these problems we would settle them in a very short time because we all know what they are.
We spent a substantial amount of money on storage charges for feed grain. Yet I am told that between Christmas and the 1st of February the price of grain in the Arnprior area went up $7 a ton. If it was the fault of the handler of the grain, whether it be a co-operative or a feed merchant, let us say so. Let us put the blame where it belongs. But if there was a failure to do what was necessary to get the grain into position where the farmer could have a continuous supply at an even cost, then let us do something about that and not blame somebody else. But at least let us know where the fault lies. The only way we could have found this out would have been to have the committee continue. I ask the minister why he did not do this? Is he afraid of it?
I have never seen such whitewashing organizations as the committees of the House of Commons. I do not see how anybody could be afraid of referring anything to them. The committees get so confused, so

deeply involved, they never do come to any decision. I have sat on many committees but I never sat on one that made a constructive or comprehensive decision. These are two of the things that were suggested. What does the agriculture committee concern itself with now? I am not talking about the beginning of the session, but now, at a time when the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has said we have to pass 37 new items or we do not have any summer holiday. At this time we are being asked to sit in a committee as well, so that we can get that out of the way.
There are problems in agriculture, but we should start doing something about them. I have a particular problem in my area that concerns me very much. I refer to the matter of credit, and I have heard the minister say a great deal about credit. I am not speaking about the farmer who can get credit from a bank, but about the farmer who cannot get credit anywhere. I am speaking of the farmer who has to increase his unit in order to make an economic unit that will produce enough agricultural products to provide his family with a living, and him with enough money to repay his loan. This seems to me to be the field in which the federal government must act in extending farm credit. It is in this field that they have failed. I could say they have failed for many reasons, and one of them might be the patronage that has been involved in the legal work connected with the extension of farm credit.
I do not believe this is true. On the other hand, I do not believe it is entirely without foundation. The situation is no better with Conservative lawyers than with Liberal lawyers. Both of them have been exceptionally slow in processing applications. In northern Ontario we have snow for about six months of the year and conditions are such that you cannot do the actual evaluation of properties. If the local people hold up an application and the season in which the evaluation can be made goes by, then that evaluation is delayed sometimes a year or 18 months. This has happened many times. Few of the farmers in my area are wealthy. Their farm units are small, about 150 acres. Many of them have a substandard of living on this small income. Some farmers supplement their income by working at odd jobs on the highways or in the bush during the wintertime. They are interested in developing an economic unit that will provide for their families. When they ask the Farm Credit Corporation for a loan of $2,000 or $3,000, the corporation says the loan cannot be extended because the farmer would not have an economic unit.
These farmers are living on these units and raising families. They must consider them to
25, 1964
Eastern Agricultural Assistance be economic units. One of the great drawbacks arises from the fact that the department has been valuing land at about $25 per acre. In northern Ontario clearing the land costs about $50 an acre. If it costs $50 an acre to clear land, then I think it would be poor business if that land did not become worth $50 an acre. Then, of course, one gets into the ARDA program and the question of whether or not this land should have become agricultural land, or whether it should have been developed for something else. Perhaps if the minister were to extend credit for a shorter term on small amounts, the farmers could get started and it would be of great help to the farmers.
I do not make the suggestion that I know the answer to this problem. I may be wrong in wanting to extend small loans to farmers for a shorter period of time to enable them to buy the farm across the road for $3,000 or $5,000. However, I believe the minister is wrong in saying it is not possible to do this. The committee should meet so that we could hear the experts in this field who would be able to tell us what the situation would be if this type of credit were established on a regional basis. I know hundreds of farmers in my area who would be helped by loans of $1,000 or $2,000 if this type of credit were established to permit them to purchase additional land in the locality.
I am sure the same conditions apply in Quebec. There is a similarity between agriculture in northern Ontario and in parts of northwestern Quebec. I feel that farm credit could be extended on a regional basis with better results than are now achieved under the Farm Credit Corporation. If you do not ask for $25,000 when you make an application to the Farm Credit Corporation, they think you are nuts; you are not really in the farming business and you are not working an economic unit.
I can assure you there are many workers in Canada who would like us to permit Household Finance Corporation to make loans of $10,000 to householders. If we did this, we would only compound their problems and they would owe $10,000 instead of $2,000. This would not be a good thing. If some of the farmers in my area were to borrow $25,000, they would be putting their children under a mortgage for a lifetime. I do not believe this would be an advantageous thing. It might not be desirable, and it might not meet the needs of many of my people.
I receive many letters asking me for assistance in connection with farm credit problems. These people get a heck of a lot more assistance from the junior farm loan board in Ontario than they do from the

Eastern Agricultural Assistance Farm Credit Corporation. I feel that is a disgrace because the federal government is in a position to extend credit to a greater degree than that which is extended by Ontario, where there is an age limit for the applicant.
There are many other problems in agriculture, and there are a few that the minister does not know about. There is one to which I should like to ask him to give consideration and that is the change in the cheese subsidy. He lowered the subsidy by one cent. The cheese producers, in my opinion, have done an excellent job of disposing of their own product. They seem to have been in the same position as the wheat pools, the Canadian wheat board, and yes even the minister, in connection with selling wheat. They have been able to go into the external markets and sell their products. It is gratifying to find that Canadian Cheddar cheese is at a premium of 8 cents or 10 cents per pound on the English market. I think it is gratifying to the Canadian producers, and it must be gratifying also to those who are interested in agriculture products to find that last year cheese exports to Great Britain amounted to between four million and five million pounds. This has been accomplished by the farmer in co-operation with the federal government, which has granted a subsidy of four cents. I understand the minister has dropped the subsidy by one cent.
We may be confused, and certainly the minister may be, by the problem of getting rid of surplus agricultural products. He may have been confused by the fact that we are getting rid of the butter oil surplus. I say, however, that we are not getting rid of it; we have thrown it away. It is very simple to figure out the amount of storage we pay each year. At the end of a few years storage costs amount to 15 cents, and after that, when you ship it some place and sell it for 27 cents there is no money for the federal government in such a process. I do not say that we should not give it away, but let us not get confused about it and think that we have done a good job. There comes a time when I have to liquidate my car because it is not economical for me to keep it any longer. It may be the same with our butter oil. It may be that we should not hold on to it any longer, but let us not tell everybody that we made 27 cents out of it, because we did not make anything out of it.
We can upset the balance in the dairy industry very easily by playing with one particular commodity. Over the years there was a good export market for Canadian Cheddar cheese, but we are all aware of the fact that we loused that market up in Great Britain and that it took a great deal of effort to get

it back. The Ontario cheese producers have spent a lot of their own money in Great Britain promoting the sale of Cheddar cheese, and the Ontario cheese marketing board has done an excellent job, with the co-operation of the government through the subsidy it paid. I would like the minister to stand up and justify the stopping of that one cent subsidy. That subsidy would not cost the Canadian people millions of dollars, but it does cost them $50 million to subsidize butter.
The minister has some fairly good advisers and I would like to compliment one of them, Mr. Phillips, who seems to know a great deal about the Department of Agriculture. In fact, I may say he is alone in knowing anything about it, because quite a few people in it have not been able to give information to members of the public v/ho went to the department seeking information. I believe this official could do very well if he were promoted to a top public relations job, mainly because he is willing to find out some of the problems that exist in the department, and the solutions for them.
In my opinion the minister will have to justify the dropping of this one cent subsidy. Is it not a matter of pride to him that we can export raw milk cheese to Great Britain? Is it his desire to have a price competition take place between New Zealand and Canada, so that either the importers in England will not hold our cheese long enough to give it the seasoning it needs, or the sale to them will take place on the basis of different prices over the contract year?
One of the reasons that we have been able to sell our cheese so successfully is that we have had a contract price that applied over the year, not taking into consideration the delivery date. A subsidy of four cents has brought about this situation, and I think the minister should continue that subsidy.
My father has spent a lifetime in the dairy industry in eastern Canada and he informs me that the most complex problem existing today is that we have not been able to pool milk in Ontario, and there has been a fight taking place between the concentrated milk industry, the whole milk industry and the processed milk industry. They must have an integrated relationship between their costs of production, and unless the whole industry is organized under one marketing agency this situation will continue. The minister should know this. Surely he did not drop that one cent subsidy so that he could save the money on the whole stabilization program? If he did, then I say it is a very expensive economy and one that we should not be making.

I have not made any suggestions because I do not really think that agriculture is a subject for a vote of confidence in the government. This government has not changed anything except to drop the one cent subsidy I have been speaking about. We can drift along for the next few years without improving the situation, so long as great changes are not made, and the question of confidence rests on whether or not the government is capable of giving leadership in agriculture.
The farmer has scratched along for many years and will probably be able to carry on for a few more years. The question is whether the government is able to give the necessary leadership. To date it has not, and I believe I am fair in saying that.
The Conservatives have been able to travel on ARDA for a long time. That is a very good piece of legislation, and it may be that the government is right in separating ARDA from the Department of Agriculture. ARDA is a long range program, but in my opinion it will never solve all the agricultural problems of the farmer. It is a program designed to put agricultural land back into more profitable production than hitherto existed under marginal farming in eastern Canada. It is a long range program, and the only question is what the government is going to do about it today.
The idea of ARDA was very good. I supported it and thought it an excellent long range program, but in my area it has become a political weapon. If you vote Conservative you are apt to get your cattle placed on the community pasture, but if you don't you won't. The reason is because Ontario runs the ARDA program, not the federal government. As with many things, the federal government has given it up to the province. The federal government does not believe in strong centralized government and in a strong centralized ARDA program; it believes in decentralization.

maintopic: REALIZED NET FARM INCOME IN CANADA
speechtext: Tell it to the Tory cows.

maintopic: REALIZED NET FARM INCOME IN CANADA
speechtext:
It has become a Tory cow in my area. As a matter of fact, I recall the story of a well known merchant in my area who brought in seed potatoes and offered them to the farmers to grow for him, but it did not turn out that way because the fertilizer costs were as much as his share of the crop. Those people now want to buy cows to put them on the community pasture, and this sort of thing is taking place all the time.
I do not really think the amendment is a question of confidence in the government. I have heard the story that the minister is a slow starter. In fact I think he repeated it 20220-226i
Eastern Agricultural Assistance himself. He is a well known international auctioneer, and in this context may I say I am always amused when a drunk stands up at an auction and tries to give the auctioneer a hard time. This also sometimes happens at political meetings, but I have never known an auctioneer to be troubled by that type of person. If the minister is a slow starter I hope he will be able to come back with the answers and provide the repartee that is necessary. The question of confidence rests on whether the government is going to take early action. The minister himself has mentioned the four things with which the amendment is concerned. He has said these are the problems that face our farmers and he has personal knowledge of them. I have personal knowledge of them, too, as has every person in this house who was raised on a farm. These problems, as we all know, are farm machinery, stabilization of income, feed grains, a pasture policy, and water conservation. We each have some knowledge of these matters. The vote of confidence will be called on whether or not in the very near future the minister is prepared to bring legislation before parliament that will solve, for the farmers of Canada, some of these very important agricultural problems.

maintopic: REALIZED NET FARM INCOME IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have again today an opportunity to discuss agriculture. This reminds me that on several occasions farmers in my riding pointed out that there were many references to agriculture made in this house, but that there were very few results.
I think that we have again an opportunity to deal with agriculture in our country more especially, since such is the subject matter of the non-confidence motion: the problem of agriculture in eastern Canada, that is in Ontario, in the province of Quebec and the maritime provinces.
I feel that we should admit, as stated by the former minister of agriculture, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), that agriculture is a basic problem in Canada, since we have always been concerned with agriculture and its related problems. I feel that this is a basic problem. It must be recognized just the same that agriculture is also a basic industry and that we depend on it to a large extent.
This brings me to the main point of the discussion, namely that, in our country, agriculture seems to be the only industry in which the producer is not sure of making a profit on his product.
In general, an uneconomic industry does not survive. It disappears immediately. But this is impossible for agriculture.

Eastern Agricultural Assistance
How is it that, in Canada, an industry as widespread and long standing as agriculture, and established throughout the country, is uneconomic for those concerned, for the farmers themselves?
Why is it that the industry in general can set for its product a price including a profit, whereas the farmer, the man who produces and feeds the country, cannot set the price of its product, including in it the profit he is entitled to just like any other producer?
That of course raises a point which is related to farm organization as well as to numerous farm associations throughout the country, which makes it very difficult to unite them. Consequently, it is difficult also to get all the farmers to accept an agricultural policy that would enable them to control the sale of their own products in order to benefit from it themselves, and not leave the profit to middlemen who are not producers but just professionals in haggling and trade who benefit from the farm industry at the expense of the producer and the consumer.
I know that in the province of Quebec in particular the problem of agriculture is truly acute because the value of farms has been decreasing for a number of years. That situation is due to several factors, the main one being the steady increase in production costs.
Farmers had to face a period of automation, a rise in the prices of by-products and a rise in taxes. They had to face all kinds of increases. They had to adjust by themselves to a general increase in the standard of living, while at the same time, their income could not keep up with that general increase.
I believe that in view of the fact that farming in Quebec is quite special, because it was based formerly on the family farm, covering a small area, it must be recognized that the farm problem in eastern Canada, and in Quebec in particular, requires very special attention.
In the province of Quebec the farming industry is confined mainly to the butter and cheese production. The Quebec dairy industry is for the farmer the main source of income.
When, once in a while, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) announces with great satisfaction that he has succeeded in amending regulations in the field of agriculture to make savings I wonder who has asked him to reduce the expenditures of his department. I cannot think of a single instance where an hon. member, a group or an association in Canada brought pressure to bear on the federal government for some reduction in the estimates of the Department of Agriculture.
If there is one federal department which is absolutely necessary and which requires more money, it is the Department of Agriculture.

In my opinion, it is absolutely out of proportion to spend something like $180 million on agriculture at present, whereas defence expenditures total the fantastic amount of $1,500 million.
I can certainly assure the minister that he will never have to face reprisals in the house for having authorized his department to draw larger amounts from the national treasury if these funds are used to help our farmers. I can also assure him that he will always obtain the support of all the members of this house.
Recently, he announced certain amendments to the regulations concerning cheese and butter. This leads me to raise a point which is particularly interesting for the dairy producers of Quebec, that is the quotas which apply to them. The fluid milk producer who delivers his product as such for consumption is submitted to delivery quotas. These delivery quotas do not cover his entire production and surpluses must be used for cheese production. In that case, he is not entitled to any assistance or grant because he is allowed a quota for fluid milk. In my opinion, it would be advisable to amend these regulations and to see that farmers who are selling fluid milk up to 400 or 500 pounds are granted the same rights and subsidies for milk delivered for cheese production, because at the present time, they do not receive any assistance from the government for their 300 or 400 pounds of surplus. This is completely discriminatory and unfair, since we are not helping the farmers.
The minister reduced the assistance with one hand and he increased it with the other to induce the cheese makers to produce a better quality cheese. If it is the minister's intention, through such a policy, to encourage the production of a better quality cheese, I am all for it, and I am convinced besides that all the producers and farmers in the dairy industry and in the cheese industry in particular, agree that this objective be followed so that we get a quality production which will be easier to market. In addition, even while trying to help the farmer to do better, I think that the minister has no right to deprive him from an extra income by reducing the assistance which he offers him in another field. If he wants to encourage him to do better, let him offer him more. To reduce the assistance with one hand while increasing it with the other, does not show much discernment.
I hope that the minister will strive to adapt his policy in that respect, because I think that in the months or even the days ahead, he will have to face the general outcry of the farmers' associations from the province of

Quebec who will come here in order to make their point with regard to that new policy. I became convinced of it after reading the resolutions which appeared in the newspapers in my own area-and which were carried by the farmers' associations-dealing with the effects of that new government's decision.
We want to increase farm production, we want to make farming more stable economically; but then we have to provide markets to our farmers. We want our farms to expand and to become mechanized so as to produce more. Why? We know that according to statistics, there are surpluses already.
Mr. Speaker, it is useless to urge our farmers to increase their production if we are unable at the same time to ensure markets for their products so that they might sell them at a fair price. I feel that the Minister of Agriculture, in co-operation with the minister of trade (Mr. Sharp), should strive to find markets for farmers.
I should like to suggest to the minister that he read the reports given to the papers recently by his predecessor, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, following his trip to China where he apparently found tremendous markets for Canadian farmers.
Everybody here knew that those markets existed. We all knew that those markets existed in mainland China and that over 600 million Chinese are starving, a great number of whom are doing without the bare minimum. It is obvious that there is a market in China for the Canadian farm production.
Incidentally, I should like, at this stage, to point out to the minister that there is room for more consumers here in Canada, as there are surely Canadians who are still not getting the three meals a day to which they have a right. I suggest that the Minister of Agriculture and his colleagues should take a sympathetic interest in our farmers, especially those who are at present suffering the greatest hardships.
You are aware of the fact that the Saguenay region, where I come from, as well as the province of Quebec, is going through hard times. It has long been said that the Saguenay region was blueberry country. Well, Mr. Speaker, I regret to say that this has not been true for a number of years.
It has been the fame of the area for a long time but it is now a thing of the past, since that industry moved into the maritimes. We even have some colleagues who are amongst the most important producers. It seems that this industry is very prosperous in the maritimes. Besides, the Saguenay has everything to revive it, if markets can be secured. There certainly is a great potential for the production of blueberries, and that
Eastern Agricultural Assistance potential still exists, but unfortunately, the markets have completely disappeared because the Canadian government has shown no interest whatsoever in that production and has never tried to secure markets. Some swindlers got busy securing control on the American markets so as to force producers, let alone pickers, as they are called in the industry, to accept absurdly low prices for their work. So it is that today, the Saguenay people are in no way interested in picking blueberries, because they know that they cannot secure a reasonable price.
I know that the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier), who represents the area, supports my remarks, because in both our counties, ARDA, which is worth-while legislation, has made every effort to revive the production of blueberries and promote their sale.
Moreover, again last week, people desirous to work in the blueberry fields were telling me: All this is very well, but where are we going to sell our production, since we have no assurance that it will be better and that we will be able to obtain a reasonable price. That is the question.
What is the purpose of producing if there are no consumers, no one who can purchase the goods at a reasonable price? That is the point and it is only when we are assured of a reasonable market price that we will be able to solve the problem of production because as such production does not constitute a problem. Advise producers to produce and forget the rest. There can be no doubt about that considering the present competition between farmers.
If the Minister of Agriculture wants millions of pounds of cheese and millions of bags of potatoes, he is going to get them. He asked western farmers to produce wheat. He told them: "Produce wheat and we shall sell it." Now that they have done so he does not dare sing the same tune. Why? Obviously because western farmers did produce a little too much and, at one time, the federal government was stuck with a surplus.
Now, if the Minister of Agriculture were to ask Quebec farmers to produce butter, cheese or any other commodity, he would be sure of getting enough to flood the world markets because the soil is good and our farmers are willing to work. In fact, they are willing to work providing they get reasonable compensation for their efforts, just like industrial workers in general and any other kind of workers.
Mr. Speaker, even though dairy production is very important in the Saguenay area, for some time now our farmers have turned to other fields of endeavour because they were asked to cut down dairy production.

Eastern Agricultural Assistance
Many launched out into the poultry industry others into the broiler industry and others still took up pig breeding. But all of them are facing exactly the same problem, the same difficulty, that is the price of the product ready for market.
On the other hand, the problem is closely related to the price of feed grains.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to point out that in the Saguenay region we are, of course, somewhat far from other big feed grain centres, but I believe we are still entitled to some consideration. For the two years we have been in this house, under both the previous and present administration, we have advocated a feed grain policy which would permit eastern farmers, those of Quebec province and especially those of the Saguenay region, to compete on the larger markets to sell their finished products.
However, this policy seems to be very complex, as, after two years' study, we recently learned from the very mouth of the Minister of Agriculture that it would only be announced next fall.
Yet, for many years the farmers have approached the federal authorities and submitted many a brief suggesting solutions for the various farm problems in eastern Canada. In fact, I am certain that the departmental files are full of briefs submitted to the minister and to his predecessor. There certainly would be some solutions for those problems in those briefs. Moreover, those briefs were submitted by people in the agricultural field, and I think that the minister should not ask the opinion of Tom, Dick and Harry but rather that of those people who-from a technical point of view, I would say-are in the best position to solve their own problems by submitting appropriate suggestions and recommendations.
They want legislation that will solve those problems and it is such legislation they want us to pass in this house; it seems that it is the very legislation which the present government, as well as the former one, wants to delay, for reasons they do not want to tell us and for which they are unwilling to give favourable consideration to the claims of the eastern farm organizations.
Their main claim at this time concerns the establishment of a feed grain agency for the east. This claim seems to me hardly excessive. Indeed, the western farmers asked for a grain board and obtained it. Since then, their problems seem to have been partially settled and their economic situation has much improved. I am not trying to say they are millionaires but their financial position has definitely improved.
The eastern farmers want a feed grain agency in order to avoid being exploited-
[Mr. Lessard (Lake St. John) .1
and I mean exploited-by the middle men, those shrewd businessmen, the professional farmers of St. James street who have never seen a cow in their whole life, who have never even set foot in a field and who, in their big well-designed offices, set the prices of goods going from the producer to the consumer.
They are the people we should expose. They have often and again been denounced, but nothing has been done up to now to correct this situation. Why? Because those millionaires, of course, manage to be heard when they lobby the government with lawyers at their side. They are stronger than the farmers.

speechtext: That is right.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those people have a very strong voice. As a matter of fact, it was even reported in certain newspapers that there was a lobby in Ottawa, that the members of parliament were the last to be consulted in this matter and that, whenever those people came to see us, it was because all other means had failed.
Mr. Speaker, lobbying has been practised ever since parliament began, and those who practice it are unquestionably stronger than the small farmers from the back concessions. Moreover, we found out last year what millionaires and brokers could do and how influential they were. As a matter of fact, one of them succeeded after a very short visit in having an act amended. Yet no matter how many visits our farmers make they do not succeed in bringing about much change.
We saw the result of lobbying last year; we still see it today. It is regrettable that our governments cannot, once and for all, decide to treat all Canadians on an equal footing. They yield, they give way to pressures if they are strong enough; but when they are not, then they protect their own friends.
Last year, the Saguenay district farmers had to borrow over $2 million from the Farm Credit Corporation, the money being used to mechanize their farms following the government's advice to expand their farms in order to make them more profitable and increase production. But later the government told them to cut down dairy production because there were surpluses. We must admit that it is somewhat illogical as far as policy is concerned.
Mr. Speaker, the farmer who works from 12 to 18 hours a day, receives very little for his labour, if we consider the salary paid the industrial worker who has little skill compared to the farmer.
The farmer has to be a jack-of-all-trades. He must be something of a lawyer, to protect himself adequately. He must be a specialist

in all fields, and yet he does not get much in return for all those skills and knowledge. Our lives depend on him; he puts on our table the food we eat. And what consideration have we got for him? I wonder. If the farmer should decide tomorrow to stop producing, I think we would all be in a fine fix.
At any rate the problem has reached the point where, at a meeting in the Saguenay area, the farmers unanimously passed a resolution in which they threatened not to pay their taxes. Things have come to that.
Out of 168 farmers present at a meeting, 168 decided they would no longer pay their municipal and school taxes. We have reached that point, and the situation is serious.
The farmer has to pay a great deal more in taxes than the ordinary citizen. It should not be so, since his production brings him less income. But such is the situation that he has to bear the brunt of our whole system and foot the bill for all the blunders that can be made.
The Department of Agriculture is in the process of being subdivided. Some jurisdiction has been given to the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), in whom I have confidence, because he is from Quebec. Not that I want to hold against the present Minister of Agriculture the fact that he is not from eastern Canada, but being an easterner himself, the Minister of Forestry is in a better position to understand the situation.
Now, that leads me to wonder, since we have had western ministers of agriculture who were interested in grains and who worked out the grain problem, and since the present Minister of Agriculture, who is interested in livestock, seems to be working out the livestock problems, whether we will soon have a minister of agriculture directly and personally involved in the dairy industry, because then he would probably know what he is talking about and might co-operate in order to settle the problems in that field.
Since we had men experienced in other areas, I hope that before long, we will have a minister with some experience in the dairy industry.
The present Liberal government has been in power for 13 months. Of course, if we look at its record in farming, we do not find, unfortunately, a long list of achievements. I wish I could find one because destructive criticism is not interesting. I should like to make constructive and objective criticism in the light of achievement in agriculture. Unfortunately, in 13 months, even if we recognize that they had other fish to fry, that one was not done. It may be that the Liberal party had no special training in farming matters; they were undoubtedly better qualified in industry
Eastern Agricultural Assistance and public relations, but I believe and I hope that with the advent of a new minister in that field, in whom I have confidence because I think he has imagination, something will be undertaken. Will he succeed? I do not know, but I think he will undertake something and 1 have confidence because he is a man of decision.
I hope he will get his information from the proper place and that after obtaining it he will take action so that our eastern farmers can be equal partners in Canada with equal opportunities in their profession.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out that at the present time, ARDA is the only legislation to which attention is being paid, the only legislation that seems to be accepted as a solution. It is the only one that is applied in eastern Canada at this time and incidentally, I wish to commend the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) who was minister of agriculture when that legislation was passed. The Liberal government are enforcing it with even more energy and I wish to congratulate them, because they are trying to improve it. I think that that legislation should not be the only one to deal with the problem. There are other measures which have to be passed if we want eastern farmers to be assured of a fair return for their daily work, as in the case of other sectors of the Canadian industry.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to take the floor again on the matter of agriculture; I have already discussed the subject several times in the house and I do not know whether my remarks will have the same effect, because when one speaks of agriculture-especially along the lines of this amendment concerning agriculture in the east-one gets the impression that he is talking to a brick wall.
When one knows all the needs of the province of Quebec, I can assure you that when one speaks in the house or has correspondence with some departments, one gets the impression that for some people, eastern agriculture is not much indeed in the Canadian economy.
I listened to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) while he was dealing with agriculture and I pictured him with the new Canadian flag in his hand, because he first spoke of our national flag. I congratulate him because he admitted most sincerely in this house that he was in favour of a distinctive flag. I congratulate also all those who support this project, of the English as well as the French element. I somewhat blame those who look too far behind and completely forget to look ahead. I feel

Eastern Agricultural Assistance that the flag, whatever its design, for I know it will be selected by competent men, and that is why we voted for a distinctive flag, will be the beginning of the new confederation in the union of both elements of this nation.
We always had and always will have reactionaries, but the French element is the one which always moderated its pretentions and sacrificed its own personality to try and make a success of the great Canadian cause.
We wish that the English refractory element, which is still against this project, would think a little more of the nation. It wants it to be great, but in its own way. As for us, we want the nation to be as it ought to be: great, unique, and it must have a distinctive emblem. I believe that we will have this distinctive emblem in a few days-at least I wholeheartedly wish it-and I hope that the discussion on this matter will not last forever and kill such a fine project.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle wanted to suggest that this question was a smokescreen behind which the government endeavoured to hide its shortcomings. In my opinion, each party had its failures, its strong points and weak points, when it was in office. It is a matter of getting rid of the bad, salvaging the little good there is and trying to do better.
In my opinion, that is a rather strong attack against an initiative towards unity which should gain the confidence of all members of the house.
We point out readily the good there was: when they were in office, the Conservatives did a lot for agriculture, especially the bill to set up a department of agriculture for eastern Canada, and ARDA. We are grateful to them and we appreciate their work. But, after passing such legislation they announced that the 25 cents premium per hundredweight of milk was to be abolished. We, from Quebec, had to swallow that much more. That measure was not good for Quebec, the farmers protested and sent telegram after telegram; they changed nothing and we had to accept that.
Now, the Liberals are in power and they also have their good and bad points. They started by killing the bill to set up an eastern department of agriculture which is essential to Quebec, and I think that the province of Quebec will never get over that.
Now, they gave us a semblance of a department of forestry. They probably compare agriculture in Quebec to a wide forest, since they transferred this minister into forestry; let us hope he may produce something for Quebec.
I am one of those who firmly believes that a single thing will save Quebec: the enact-

ment by this parliament of a piece of legislation to give Quebec a department which will directly control agriculture in that province. I discussed the matter on several occasions and I mentioned it a few moments ago; those who are acquainted with Quebec know very well that today a minister coming from the west, a minister who thinks and dreams only about wheat, cannot understand the province of Quebec. It is impossible. Let us not expect the impossible. For him it is impossible to try to understand the province of Quebec and its family farming. They say that Quebec should be modernized and its lands should be expanded.
There is one thing I do not understand: it is that 100 or 150 years ago, most of our farmers came to settle on these lands because they were rich lands, real agricultural lands. At that time the west was never mentioned. All those farmers came to establish themselves especially in the Lake St. John and the Quebec areas, saying they were settling down in the granary of agriculture.
Today, all of a sudden, that granary is being converted into a desert, according to the idea or the semblance of idea which the ministers have conceived about it in the course of the last 50 years. I wonder why those ministers have not come to see what was going on in the province of Quebec in that respect.
Besides, I notice something else. If, here in this house, the impression prevails that the Quebec lands are poor, it is perhaps due to the fact that for 50 years, there was no minister of agriculture who would go and investigate for himself the farming situation in the province of Quebec. For 50 years, parliament took pleasure in choosing ministers from the west. I bear no grudge against my colleagues. They did right, they had a majority.
But today, if everybody, if all members of the house seem willing to solve this problem-we feel they truly want to rehabilitate the province of Quebec-then let us do something, let us create an efficient weapon designed to help solve the farming problem in Quebec. I feel that the only efficient weapon is to set up for eastern Canada a department that will look after forests and mines and also land and farming.
As a matter of act, what is lacking in our province? First of all, drainage. Hundreds of millions of dollars were spent to drain the land in the prairie provinces. I have not yet seen a single cent allocated for that purpose in the province of Quebec, and yet the citizens of Quebec know how much their province, especially the land in the Lake St. John and Saguenay areas, is in need of drainage.

We might get a few thousand dollars for drainage in 1965, according to a statement made by Quebec's minister of agriculture. I wrote to him recently, and about two weeks ago I received the particulars of a drainage project. Though ARDA has been in force for some time, we shall only start drainage projects in 1965, whereas the western provinces have already received more than $300 million to that end. Is that fair?
It might perhaps be said that the province of Quebec is lagging behind. Now Quebec is not hanging back in any way. But Quebec lacked, here in this federal parliament, the proper spokesmen to interpret and study conditions there. That is the only reason.
If we had had some responsible men in the Department of Agriculture, who had been familiar with conditions in the province of Quebec, I assure you that, they would, before now, have implemented projects satisfactory to the farmers, which at the same time would have very rapidly improved the yield of their land in a proportion of 30 to 40 per cent.
Today, we have the ARDA legislation my fellow member from Lake St. John (Mr. Les-sard), mentioned a short while ago. This legislation applies in the Lake St. John district in only two fields at this time: reforestation and blueberry growing. Broken and fully reclaimed land is taken and re-seeded to produce trees. After having laboured hard to reclaim this land from the forest it is now given back to what is now called tree farming.
As to the second project: blueberry crops. Everybody knows the Lake St. John blueberries. According to outsiders-of course when we live in this berry paradise we are unable to realize it-they are a real manna from heaven. I am saying that about 15 years ago it was a gold mine, because within a month and a half or two months, the people of Roberval riding could make $2, $3 and even $4 million.
The most interesting part of it was that such amounts were not taxable. I think that income tax inspectors were too lazy to visit the blueberries producers, and consequently that was clear profit.
On each dollar of revenue, one has today to pay 40 cents income tax, but just think that $1 is worth $1.40 for the blueberry picker, as blueberries are not taxable.
That is why I say that this industry is a real gold mine, because it is safe from any government income tax collector. Moreover, blueberries are probably picked at a certain hour of the day when tax inspectors are still in bed, and they do not have time to go to the blueberry patch.
Eastern Agricultural Assistance
At any rate, the blueberry program that we have today will surely do some good. But, as my colleague from Lake St. John pointed out earlier, the problem is to find a market. You may pick berries in 10, 12 or 15 fields of my constituency, if you cannot sell them, as I expect, the whole thing will be useless.
I discussed that problem with the minister of agriculture of Quebec and the answer he gave me was that the market would come later. But if the market comes two years after the first crop, because the first crop will be harvested this summer, I see no organization set up for the harvesting of blueberries because today, even if we had no blueberry field, Lake St. John is a region where blueberries grow wild.
If we had the market we had ten years ago; but alas, it was taken over. Taken over by whom? By the big financial interests, as they take over all the markets at all levels of our economy.
Ten or 15 years ago, we sold blueberries around $6.30 per 30 pounds, while last year, we had to sell 30 pounds of blueberries for the ridiculous price of $1.75.
And whose work is that? The work of those who have never picked a blueberry, who are resting comfortably in their easy-chairs in the big cities and who have succeeded in removing all competition. Ten or 15 years ago, we had 15, 20 or 25 buyers, whereas today there is only one who sets his own price. That reminds me of those Negroes the Americans were paying two or three cents a day to carry elephant tusks on their backs.
Blueberry pickers are paid ridiculous prices, with the result that 15 per cent of those who are able to go and pick blueberries no longer wish to do so. This is simply ridiculous.
I heard earlier the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard) say that at one time it had been a blueberry paradise. Who caused that paradise to disappear? It is the financiers who took control of the market and paid starvation wages.
Last summer, because I was under the impression that the price of blueberries had fallen on the international market, I asked someone in the blueberry business in Montreal whether the price of blueberries was higher or lower than it was ten years ago. He told me: "The price is exactly double what it was ten years ago." Blueberries are selling at twice the price they were selling ten years ago, whereas today our blueberry pickers are paid ridiculous wages for a day's work that starts at seven o'clock in the morning and ends at ten or eleven o'clock, and even at midnight.
However, many policies, such as that advocated by ARDA, can be put into practice;

Eastern Agricultural Assistance if there is no marketing policies, we will experience the same consequences and our plight will be the same as in other fields.
I remember that some 20 or 25 years ago, we used to say that we were in a position to turn out large quantities of farm products and we can still say so; the only trouble is the lack of outlets. And the government who is supposed to play the part of co-ordinator should assist farmers in marketing their products.
It is a known fact that the government is in a position to do as it pleases. When the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave his attention to the finding of markets for the western wheat, he succeeded, so I ask him today to try just as hard and not only half as hard as he did to dispose of the western wheat, with regard to the eastern products because we grow there a greater variety of products than in the west. It is the responsibility of the Minister of Agriculture, with the assistance of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, to find markets for our dairy products, such as butter, cheese, potatoes, vegetables, apples, maple syrup and so on. -Let them together find markets and our producers will not be reluctant to produce.
Once again, if depression as indicated by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, seems definitely settled in Quebec, the fault is not with the producers, but with the governments who did not support the producers' efforts to ensure reasonable cost prices and adequate markets for them. That is the reason, Mr. Speaker.
Let us cease to harass the farmer and to weigh him down with all the capital sins. Let us take our responsibilities. Let the Minister of Agriculture take his responsibilities, since he has been appointed by the government to look after agriculture throughout Canada.
Agriculture is not limited to the western provinces, it also covers eastern Canada and requests of eastern farmers must be granted.

An hon. member says that he is not deaf, but I must say that one has the impression of speaking to a group of deaf people when one is speaking here. That is why, very often, we must speak loudly. Even at that, it will not be sufficient, since I am sure nothing concrete will result from my speech. At least, the house will be aware of our needs and I will have done my duty.
Let us stop saying that farmland is poor and no longer productive in Quebec. Our farms are just as good as they were 30 years


ago. Financial interests have taken them over and have robbed our farmers of the fruits of their labour.
Farm equipment was selling for four times more than what it was worth. Just like the farmers in other parts of the country, the Quebec farmer had to modernize his farm, but had to put up with those unreasonable demands, because the banks would not make loans to farmers on easier terms at a reasonable rate of interest. Furthermore, the banks even ceased completely granting credit to our farmers who, therefore, had to go to finance companies and borrow at a rate of 17, 18 and even 30 per cent interest, which the government was tolerating. That is what ruined the farmers and, Mr. Speaker, I know what I am talking about because I lived through it.
And if we needed a machine that was worth $100, we began by paying $400; with the interest, it cost us $600. That is the work of finance in agriculture in the province of Quebec.
On the other hand, I know that western farmers may have certain difficulties about prices, but they are less serious, because all members of the cabinet and the minister are working for them, including the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) who is trying to sell their commodities and get reasonable prices for them.

LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying when we adjourned at six o'clock, the present agricultural stagnation in the province of Quebec results from lack of markets and a lack of initiative on the part of the government in order to support the efforts of our producers, who are ready to produce 25 per cent more provided their products sell at profitable prices.
I concluded by denouncing the invasion of our Quebec farms by financiers. In fact, the farmers could not borrow from the banks at reasonable rates, the amounts necessary to purchase modern equipment, and they had to sacrifice everything to financial interests so as to survive modernism. Rates as high as 20, 24 and even 30 per cent were being claimed; during that time our governments were asleep. If, by any chance, somebody woke up, it was to tell our farmers to stop buying farming equipment.
Today we have farm credit. Thanks to this farm credit, our farmers may perhaps produce more, but nevertheless profitable markets are necessary. I hope the government will understand in time-

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Somebody on the other side says that, in addition to farm credit, we also have Social Credit. I hope that one day farm credit will fall under the control of Social Credit, and then we shall see our farmers prosperous.
At present, farm credit helps only a very small number of farmers, because with politics and patronage here like everywhere else, I may say that the future of agriculture soon takes second place, and the old greedy man quickly comes to the surface.
It is also through government action in co-operation with farmers, and not through socialization, but by supporting the individual efforts of each and everyone, thanks to private enterprise, that Quebec will be able to survive from the economic standpoint.
For instance, let our co-operatives deal directly with western producers. Let our eastern farmers pay for feed grain the same price this government sells it to red China. In brief, let us do without the financiers and help, by a protective action, eastern farmers to deal with those of the west. Let us have a price policy for eastern products. Besides, that is precisely what gave the west its high agricultural level. Indeed, the government helped western farmers by guaranteeing them
Eastern Agricultural Assistance such really economic prices which make impossible financier competition such as we have in Quebec.
When our farmers succeed in producing something, there is a rush of financiers to our farmers every fall. At this time, we have no organization which could act in cooperation with the government in order to ensure really economic prices for our farmers.
Let us set up this policy in Quebec. Let us protect farm prices and establish markets for the merchandising of their crops.
As I said, we always take example on western Canada because, especially during the last 30 years, the government has spent huge sums of money to help western producers and I say that it was a good thing. But what we did wrong was to forget the province of Quebec completely. We are not asking today to multiply the joint programs which, although they were very well received in the western provinces, are nevertheless completely contrary to the ideal of the Quebec farmer.
Special legislation should be introduced for the province of Quebec, since special legislation was enacted to help the western provinces; give Quebec an even break and help the Quebec farmer with legislation to his stature.
That is what we are asking. We are not asking for more than the other provinces have received. We are simply asking to be treated as they were. Legislation favourable to the province of Quebec should be introduced, legislation from which our farmers will benefit, just like western provinces have benefited from legislation made for them. We are asking for action based on the views and the co-operation of all our local and provincial farm organizations.
I hope that this time we are not talking to deaf ears, as in past years, and that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) will decide some day, which is yet to come, to glance towards the province of Quebec and show, at least in this parliament, that he is really the Minister of Agriculture for the whole of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to participate in a discussion of the problems of eastern agriculture. We found very interesting the remarks made this afternoon by the former minister of agriculture, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton). It did seem a little hypocritical to those of us who sit on this side of

Eastern Agricultural Assistance the house when the hon. member attached so much criticism and blame to the government and to the minister for failing to cure the ills of eastern agriculture in one year when his government was unable to do anything about it in a period of six years. I am not minimizing the problems of agriculture in eastern Canada. They are many and their roots are quite deep, as are any solutions which may be offered to solve those problems.
From listening to the hon. member this afternoon it was difficult to tell whether he was going to move a motion of criticism of this government or of the dominion bureau of statistics. On some occasions he was telling us that the farmers should pay attention to certain sets of figures which have been provided, and in the next breath he was telling us we should disregard the figures which have been provided. If the hon. member for Qu'Appelle represented an eastern agricultural riding as I do he would not need statistics to indicate to this house or to anybody else that there are serious problems facing the farmers in eastern Canada.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Then why don't you do something about them?

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
If the hon. member will give us an opportunity we will certainly do something about them.
I have spoken on two occasions, Mr. Speaker, since coming to this house about eastern agriculture and I have not spared the government that criticism which I thought it merited and deserved. But at the same time I think it is most unusual for a former minister of agriculture-and this is the second occasion on which he has done so-to stand up in this house and move a motion of censure against this government for a situation which his government failed to correct in the six years they were in office.
Besides supplying long lists of statistics to back up his argument, which I am not disputing, the former minister took considerable time to tell the members on this side of the house that we should not go into or review the past. I do not intend to go back into the past and talk about the record of the previous government because I think that is well known; the very statistics which the former minister presented both on this occasion and on a former occasion indicate the complete failure of the previous government to give any assistance to the farmers in eastern Canada. The income statistics which he mentioned and which he put on the record on the occasion when the question was debated last fall, on October 14, clearly indicate that this is not a problem which has arisen within the last year. The minister admitted very clearly

that it has existed in eastern Canada for several years, and the statistics he quoted also indicate very clearly that his government failed, and failed miserably, to do anything about it.
I said a moment ago that the former minister cautioned us not to review the past, and I will certainly follow that advice. It is never our intention to be critical of the past, and I think hon. members on this side are to be commended for the decision which they have taken not to go into the past. We do not want to thresh old straw; we want to get on with something more concrete and talk about what this government has done for the eastern farmers and what it plans to do if given the opportunity. I think the members of the opposition have an excellent opportunity to show their good will to and their concern for the farmers of eastern Canada by co-operating with the government and letting us get on with the legislation which is on the order paper, as well as other legislation which the minister wants to bring before the house to benefit the farmers in eastern Canada.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE

I know that members in all parts of the house-I am not being critical of the members of the opposition- are concerned at the plight of the farmers in eastern Canada, and I am sure they will co-operate with the government in getting this legislation enacted so that those farmers can stand to benefit by it.
