maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: You made the remark that you had brought down so much for agriculture. What have you done for agriculture?

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the question and I will mention two things which we have done. Other speakers from this party will expand and indicate other measures which have been enacted for the benefit of the farmers in eastern Canada. I did not open my remarks, nor do I intend to continue them, in a critical vein and I think my observations so far have been in order. I do not intend to be critical in what I say and I hope I did not convey that impression. I think that what I have said is factual. The statistics which the former minister brought before the house today indicate there is a serious situation which has not been remedied for the past several years.
I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that I am convinced the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Forestry are doing an excellent job. I was at the annual meeting of the federation of agriculture at Charlottetown earlier this year, at which the Minister of Agriculture was guest speaker. The reception he received and the complimentary remarks which I have heard from all parts of my province since that time indicate that the farmers of eastern Canada are convinced that the minister is doing everything he can to improve their situation and to better their lot. More recently the Minister of Forestry, who is now responsible for the ARDA program, visited in my province, as he did in all parts of the Atlantic provinces. He received a very warm welcome. Since that time, the premier of my province has commented very favourably on the new Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) and has expressed his belief that much will be done in pursuance of the ARDA program.
Eastern Agricultural Assistance
I mentioned a few moments ago in reply to a question that I would attempt to deal with two long range actions which the government has taken so far in the interests of eastern farmers. These are the decision to create a new cabinet portfolio of forestry and rural development, and the steps taken with regard to feed grain. Attempts have been made in some quarters to suggest that the action taken in creating a new ministry cf forestry has represented a move to downgrade the federal Department of Agriculture. In fact, it has made the Department of Agriculture more important than ever. The representation of agriculture both in the cabinet and in the government as a whole has been widened by this action. It reflects the fact that our government is not a one-man operation; it does not think any one man, whether he is the Prime Minister or the Minister of Agriculture necessarily has all the answers. It also reflects the harmony which exists in our government-a seasoned harmony of reasonably minded men searching to organize government so as to reach the best possible solutions to the problems affecting agriculture in all of Canada. This government is not afraid to co-operate. It does not suffer from any delusions of omnipotence. Now, instead of a single minister trying to run everything, we have three ministers involved closely in the affairs of agriculture. It is obvious, it seems to me, that this will ensure that all aspects of agriculture are given closer attention than was possible in the past. Furthermore the special cabinet committee on agriculture, which meets frequently, sees to it that all activities in this field are co-ordinated. To suggest that the portfolio of agriculture has been downgraded is altogether misleading. The answer is obvious to all who are interested in assisting the farmers in all parts of this country: The action taken by the government in this respect is one which is bound to work for the benefit of our farmers. The steps taken to ensure much closer co-ordination of farm programs are obviously designed to benefit agriculture both in the east and in the west.
As chairman of the three-minister cabinet committee, the responsibilities of the Minister of Agriculture have actually been widened. In the meantime, the new minister of forestry and rural development has to deal, in particular with two problems which are among the most urgent currently facing eastern farmers. One of these is the cost of feed grain and the other is the question of the efficient use of land. The present government has already taken steps to solve each of these problems and further action is being considered. It is well known that steps were taken last year

Eastern Agricultural Assistance -last August, to be exact-to encourage stability of supply and price in eastern Canada, conditions which had not existed with respect to feed grain in years past. Although the action is well known, perhaps it is not as well understood as it might be. I propose, therefore, to deal with this question briefly.
The livestock and poultry producers in eastern Canada depend heavily on the prairie provinces for feed grains to supplement local supplies, particularly in the winter and spring of each year. Until the present government acted to alleviate the situation, two conditions relative to storage charges discouraged grain dealers from placing adequate stocks in position in the east for winter requirements. The cost of storage itself resulted in purchases being made for delivery as late as possible in the fall in order to avoid a portion of the storage charges in the east. Then, too, the cost of storage and the relationship of the fall and spring prices on the Winnipeg grain exchange discouraged dealers from buying more than the minimum expected requirements.
Probably a word of explanation would be in order at this point. In the fall, feed dealers, including co-operatives, assess their requirements for the winter and place orders with a grain merchant for delivery prior to the close of navigation. They try to assess their requirements until the date when the first grain vessels are expected to arrive in the spring. A grain broker normally buys only to fulfil orders already made. For example, he may buy barley from the wheat board at the lakehead in October for immediate shipment to Montreal. Let us suppose he pays $1.20 a bushel. He plans to replace his stocks in the spring by purchases at the May auction. If the grain broker had received orders from feed dealers in the east amounting to say, 95,000 bushels in the fall, he might decide to take an extra 5,000 bushels just in case he found a customer during the winter after the shipping season had closed. So, he knew his cost, his selling price and his profit on the 95,000 bushels; but on the other 5,000 he had to take his chance in the winter feed grain market. If he had made an error in judgment and found he could not sell those
5,000	bushels during the winter, he would have to leave the grain in an eastern storage elevator at a cost of one cent a bushel per month. This would mean his cost per bushel would rise from the original figure of $1.20 to $1.27 plus interest charges. In due course spring comes, and barley, at the May auction is still $1.20 a bushel or perhaps even a few cents less. The broker has to take a loss on his 5,000 bushel carry-over in order to sell

it in competition with barley bought at the lower spring prices.
This was the situation until the present Minister of Agriculture moved, last fall, in co-operation with the wheat board and through the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) to correct it. Since the grain dealer, and ultimately, the farmer, had to assume the carrying costs from the moment the grain was bought, there had been a tendency, as I have explained, to delay winter purchases until near the close of navigation. This put pressure on both supplies and prices at that time. This pressure on prices often meant that the prices of oats and barley at the time of shipment in the late fall were higher than they would be the following spring. Add to this the cost of storing any carryover grain until the resumption of navigation, and hon. members will see why no broker wanted to get caught with more grains on his hands during the winter than he could sell. It was obviously safer for him to underestimate the demand than to overestimate it. It is also apparent that when this situation produced a shortage of feed grain in eastern position during the winter, the pressure on prices was always upward. If a feed merchant wanted to take advantage of such a situation, the situation was certainly there, tailor-made for him.
Within four months of the present government taking office two definite steps were taken to relieve the situation. First, the government decided to pay storage costs on western feed grains in licensed eastern elevators, from October 15 to April 15. This, of course, encouraged the purchase of a larger supply of grain for winter storage and reduced the chances of a shortage of feed grains developing in mid-winter or later. Instead of bringing in say 5 per cent more than had already been contracted for sale the broker would bring in from 10 to 15 per cent more. In a moment I will give figures to show that most eastern feed grain dealers did bring in substantially larger amounts last fall than in previous years.
With the government paying the storage from October 15, six weeks before the close of navigation, this also encouraged an earlier movement of grain from the lakehead to positions in eastern Canada. This, of course, relieved some of the pressure on shipping space and this usually means that grain can be shipped at somewhat lower lake rates, which is another saving that can ultimately be passed on to the farmers of eastern Canada.
Besides helping the farmers of eastern Canada this new policy encouraged larger purchases of western feed grain. Brokers

who previously relied on supplies of corn from United States to supplement their winter demands in this case stocked with feed grain from western Canada. With this new program of assistance the amount of western feed grain in eastern positions on November 27 last was 60 per cent higher than in any earlier year, and at the close of navigation it was almost 50 per cent higher. There were about 31 million bushels of feed grain in eastern elevators at the end of navigation last fall compared with 21 million bushels in the same positions the previous year. This build-up of western feed grain in eastern elevators earlier in the year helped to avoid the usually higher seasonal lake rates as well.
Along with the government's decision to pay the storage costs the Canadian wheat board decided to provide for deferred pricing on oats and barley for the first time. It agreed not to set the final price on replacement purchases until the grain to be replaced was leaving the eastern storage elevator. This did a great deal to remove the uncertainty grain brokers had previously had as to the price they would have to pay for grain in the spring compared with the cost of grain in the fall.
As the figures I gave a moment ago indicate, it was apparent last November that this policy had obviously been successful in encouraging an earlier and larger movement of western feed grain to eastern storage elevators. Furthermore, in the months since then feed grain prices have remained more stable than in any previous winter.
This afternoon the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle (Mr. Hamilton) indicated that some members of his party would outline the pattern of feed grain prices in eastern Canada this past winter. While there may have been some increase in feed grain prices I think we should remember that generally prices for feed grain were probably higher this year than in previous years. I think the demand for grains generally brought about by the large sales of wheat tended to be reflected in increasing prices for grain generally, including feed grains for eastern Canada.
There are two matters which I feel stand to the credit of the government. They have been of benefit to the farmers of eastern Canada this year and we feel they will be a substantial benefit in the years to come. I mentioned a moment ago that the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), the minister now responsible for ARDA, had recently visited eastern Canada. In fact he visited all of the provinces of eastern Canada to discuss with officials there the ARDA program as it affects each of these provinces. We are convinced that ARDA holds very excellent prospects for helping the
Eastern Agricultural Assistance farmers of eastern Canada and I think that the government which brought in the legislation is to be complimented for doing so. But, Mr. Speaker, no matter how good a program it is, unless it becomes operational, unless its good features are put into action, the farmers cannot benefit from it. This is why we feel that having a minister who is able to devote his well known talents, which have already been demonstrated, to a program of this kind will make ARDA a really effective program which unfortunately, and I do not say this by way of criticism, we do not feel it has been up to this time.
In the province, of which I have the honour to represent one of the constituencies, we look forward to many accomplishments through ARDA and we feel that the action of the government in placing the talented Minister of Forestry in charge of the program indicates that the government is serious and intends to take those steps which are necessary to make ARDA an effective program, an effective weapon to deal with the difficulties facing the farmers of eastern Canada.
There are many other matters that could be discussed. As I said a moment ago, there is no easy solution to the problems of agriculture either in eastern Canada or in any other part of Canada; but this is particularly true, of course, of eastern Canada. Other speakers from the government party will speak about various phases of the program and various aspects of the problems, of which there are many. At the moment I think of the need for greater expenditure on education and research. I think also of the problem of marketing. I believe this is one of the real problems facing farmers in eastern Canada. With rising costs for everything that the farmer has to buy, rising costs of services and materials, and the almost static prices which the farmer has been receiving for his agricultural products it is not hard to conclude why his income is not what we would like it to be. This is one of the real problems that we all have to face.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: You were going to solve it.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
We will solve it and we have already taken steps in that direction. I say again that there are many problems. I started to deal with marketing. If the farmer could receive higher prices for many of the things he produces I think many of the problems he is facing at this time would soon disappear. I think particularly of the marketing of potatoes grown in my province. If we could receive throughout the year the price we are now receiving, around $2 for a 75 pound bag, many of the problems of the farmers of that province would be taken care of.

Eastern Agricultural Assistance
How far a government can go in solving these problems is something on which we might all reflect for a few moments. It is all very well to criticize any government for its failure to take action to solve problems affecting any aspect of our economy. But how far should a government go? How far, indeed, can a government go in finding a solution to the very vexing problems that affect agriculture in eastern Canada? I think we can certainly go much farther than any government has done in recent years in this country. I believe it would be well to reflect for a moment on what the governments of other countries do for agriculture. For instance, we might do well to compare our expenditures on agriculture with those of other nations with similar problems. We find that in Great Britain, for example, 7.5 per cent of the the national budget is directed to agricultural assistance. In the United States, Denmark, Sweden, Norway and France the figure is 8.2 per cent while in our country it is only 3 per cent. Compared with what these other countries spend only 3 per cent of our national budget is directed to agricultural assistance. In the same line of thought it might be well to consider the situation in terms of the percentage of the total volume of agricultural production.
In Denmark, for example, an amount equivalent to 10 per cent of the total volume of agriculture production is expended by the government to assist agriculture. In the Netherlands, it is 15.5 per cent. In Great Britain, it is 25 per cent. In the United States, our neighbour to the south, it is 14.7 per cent but in Canada, it is only 8.2 per cent. Although we do spend a great deal on agriculture, in comparison with what is done in other countries it is a relatively small amount.
I have tried, Mr. Speaker, to outline some of the problems which are affecting agriculture in eastern Canada. I have indicated at least two aspects of what this government is trying to do to solve these problems. Again, I must say that this is a matter which demands and commands the attention of hon. members in all parts of the house, and not only hon. members but people everywhere. The agriculture segment of our population, the agriculture sphere of our economy, is most important to the economy generally. I think that while there is a great deal yet to be done, this government has taken active steps to help meet the situation.
As I mentioned previously, the government has indicated by way of resolution on the order paper that it intends to do something by way of assisting in farm credit as soon as parliament can find time to deal with the matter. The minister has indicated that he

would like to do, and is prepared to do something to solve the very difficult problem of the high cost of machinery facing farmers everywhere in the country. These are matters upon which the government is prepared to act. There are many others which I know would receive sympathetic attention as soon as they can be dealt with effectively by this parliament. I mentioned some of them a moment ago. As I have said, I have not hesitated to speak clearly and frankly, both in this house and in discussion with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) and the other members of the government. I do not believe I have failed to present the very difficult problems that are facing the farmers of eastern Canada, and certainly the farmers in the riding I represent.
As I mentioned previously, if the former minister of agriculture or anybody in this house wishes to travel through eastern Canada, through the maritime provinces in particular, he will not need statistics to indicate very clearly that there is a definite problem that requires the attention of governments, of farm organizations, of private agencies or any body that is able to help the farmers. I am convinced that the present Liberal government is taking very active steps to do what is best for the farmers of eastern Canada. Our program is very clear. We are moving on that program and, with the help and co-operation of members in all parts of this house, I am sure we will move along very quickly and very effectively in solving the problems of agriculture in eastern Canada, to the benefit of the farm population in that part of the country and to the benefit of this country generally.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to give a detailed analysis of the speech made by the previous speaker, but I feel that he has taken the government at task for having botched the policies which we had set forth when we were in power and failed to keep its promises by taking the necessary steps to help farmers. During their first 60 days in power they did nothing. Yet, they had promised to help farmers.
Mr. Speaker, eastern farming is going bankrupt, the resources of our farmers are shrinking, especially under the present Minister of Agriculture. In my opinion, the government was justified in appointing an auctioneer, a man specialized in sales, because he is there to sell off farms in eastern Canada as a result of a policy of inaction followed by the government.

The income of eastern farmers is constantly declining. As an example, I refer you to d.b.s. figures concerning the net income of Quebec farmers.
For 1963, compared with 1962, the income of Quebec farmers has fallen by $5,589,000. Two thirds of Quebec farmers have an income under $1,200. Taxes increase constantly, both in Ottawa and in Quebec. The Quebec sales tax was standardized at 6 per cent, not to mention the 11 per cent tax on building materials which affects particularly eastern farmers, as well as the whole country.
Since the minister assumed office, the operating expenses of farmers have gone up unceasingly, but their income has declined constantly.
The government does not pay any attention at all to the farmers and I may tell you, Mr. Speaker, that in addition to all the problems facing the farmers, the cost of living index reached a new high in April at 135.0, that is 0.3 higher than in March, and
2.0	higher than in April 1963. The farm associations are unhappy with this government. In La Presse of April 28, 1964 I read the following:
The provincial budget does not do anything to assist the farmers.
That statement was made by Mr. Sorel, president of the Catholic farmers' union.
There was an increase in the price of milk in Montreal but it was absolutely unprofitable for the farmers, according to the Catholic farmers' union.
Land taxes increase constantly and the farmers are leaving their farms. What is the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) doing except liquidating the farms in eastern Canada, because of the present government's inaction?
Mr. Speaker, if you refer to the April 3, 1964 issue of Le Devoir, you will read this:
The Catholic farmers' union blames the federal Minister of Agriculture.
The general council of the Catholic farmers' union, at a meeting held at the Institut co-operatif Desjardins, attacked some recent statements made by the Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Hays. It requested also that the Bankruptcy Act be amended to protect the farmer against bankruptcy by a processing plant.
The Catholic farmers' union criticized a statement allegedly made recently in Winnipeg by Mr. Hays who would have expressed his formal opposition to the setting up of a feed grain board for eastern Canada and would have said that the appointment of Mr. Maurice Sauv6 to the cabinet is due to pressure from some Quebec M.P.'s.
Mr. Speaker, the government is boasting at every turn concerning the appointment of Hon. Maurice Sauve as Minister of Forestry. The appointment definitely satisfies nobody. The Canadian forestry association blamed the government for having entrusted to the Department of Forestry the responsibility of
Eastern Agricultural Assistance ARDA, while its minister is unable to devote all his time to forestry products. On the other hand, the administration of ARDA is the full responsibility of the provinces. The minister will have absolutely nothing to do in that field, except asking the house to vote sums of money.
I am asking the present Minister of Agriculture to assume his responsibilities, to wake up, to attend sittings of the house more often, in order to pay attention to repeated requests from the official opposition to help the farmer of the eastern provinces who is going bankrupt.
Mr. Speaker, I would be most happy to hear the Minister of Agriculture give a single policy he has adopted on behalf of Canadian farmers, including those of the eastern part of the country.
We had excellent policies. There was, for instance the milk subsidy of 25 cents per cwt. which the government abolished. When I asked the minister a question about that he replied that the subsidy has been removed in order to save $6 million.
I say to the federal Minister of Agriculture that he must not expect ARDA to save farmers within three, four or five years. The government must act immediately and stop sabotaging the agricultural policies we have set up.
Mr. Speaker, the first 60 days of the Liberal regime were days of mourning for Canadian farmers because our agricultural policies were undermined by the new government.
Mr. Speaker, it is essential that legislation be enacted on behalf of eastern farmers, so that more feed grain-that is grain from the western provinces-be consumed, and at less cost.
To give you an idea of the present situation, are you aware, Mr. Speaker, that 70 per cent of the beef consumed in the province of Quebec comes from outside the province? For veal, the proportion is 30 per cent; for lamb and mutton, 54 per cent; for pork, 23 per cent; for poultry, 28 per cent; for fowl and chicken, 21 per cent; for turkey, 47 per cent; and for eggs, 54 per cent. I think that the situation is the same in all eastern provinces.
It is therefore urgent for the government to carry out this legislation which was introduced under our administration, so as to adopt a permanent national policy for the economic distribution in the east of western feed grain surpluses.
Such a policy is imperative, it is requested by our farmers, by the agricultural associations representing them, and it is absolutely necessary as a starting point and as a basis for a well thought out and sound agricultural
3566	HOUSE OF
Eastern Agricultural Assistance production, which will enable the Canadian farmers to act in such a way that Canadian agriculture will play a more prominent part, while making farms more remunerative.
The function of agriculture in any country is to provide food at reasonable prices and in sufficient quantities, and contribute to the general economy of the country through its exports. Up to now, agriculture in Canada has well served this nation of ours, since we can say we are well fed and that our exports of agricultural products make up 27 per cent to 30 per cent of our whole production, thus adding its share to the general economy. This legislation respecting feed grain should help in reducing substantially the production cost of a part of the main productions in our country, that is animal production. It should also enable us to export larger quantities of more completely manufactured products than is exported at the present time.
I consider that the following reasons are fundamental and that they should receive the general approval of the house.
First, and this is addressed to the government: it is important to set a policy that will allow the western farmer to sell his crop at a price which will provide him with a reasonable income from his investment and his work, without imposing too heavy a burden on the population of the rest of the country. That legislation had precisely that common point among its many objectives.
Second, if western Canada needs a permanent policy concerning the sale of grain, eastern Canada, for the development of a more profitable agriculture, also needs a large part of those feed grain surpluses to feed its herds and establish a stable and economical livestock production.
Third, some assistance had been provided in the past few years for the transportation of grain from western Canada to eastern Canada. That policy was to be renewed each year. It has rendered tremendous services to our eastern farmers, while providing a profitable market of three million tons of grain, on the average, for the western farmer.
We would like to see the proposed legislation enacted as soon as possible by the government. This legislation would be more generous and better conceived, while eliminating to the greatest possible extent all speculation on grain. During the next few years, it would favour the establishment of a larger market for the feed grain surplus of the west, while promoting a more economical, permanent and larger animal production by the eastern farmer.
I look upon this policy, which we always wanted, the perfect complement to the fine


program of farm management, conceived by our government some time ago, which we call ARDA. Our farms, which in eastern Canada are often marginal lands, should be able to use the grain thus distributed in a more economical way, in order to increase their production by transforming it profitably on their farm, and thus adding to the fertility of a frequently poor soil and promoting the better use of an often unemployed labour force on farms which are are often too small.
In the fourth place, the legislation, once implemented by the government, would have the effect of increasing the consumption of western grain in the east, and Canadian agriculture would, because of that very fact, increase its contribution to the over-all economy of this country.
To indicate how important it is, Mr. Speaker, that this raw material we call western grain be, as much as possible, consumed in eastern Canada-I would say that in the event it is impossible to do so, it would, of course, be preferable to export a raw material like grain, but whenever possible, it would be to the advantage of this country that this raw material be transformed on Canadian farms, and more particularly on the eastern farms which have excellent pasture for that purpose.
It is always profitable, for a country like ours, to export its raw materials under as finished a form as possible. Now, when Canada exports one ton of barley, for instance, the economy is being increased by an amount of about $50. But, on the other hand, if that same ton of barley is converted in the east into beef, for instance, it can be exported, provided, of course, that the product be finished, of good quality and economically produced on the eastern farms-this finished product can be exported in the form of pork or beef and yield in this way an amount of $125 or more, according to the price presently paid for pork or beef. It would appear that an investment of $8 to $12 million by the Canadian government to economically distribute this export grain in its raw state so that it can be exported in the form of finished product, would profit to the whole of the Canadian economy. In converting that product at home, we supply work for labour at a stage where unemployment is a problem and we add at least $75 per ton to the international monetary fund.
Fifth, this national policy of economic distribution of western grain surpluses in the east is a prime requirement to balancing eastern farming.
I offered to you only a few reasons, Mr. Speaker, to show the importance of adopting

as quickly as possible some legislation promoting consumption of feed grain in eastern Canada, in order to export as little as possible to other countries.
So as to help this export of western grain to the east, I submit that the government should enact some legislation in order:
1.	To establish standard and well-balanced prices throughout the east, so as not to put at a disadvantage any user of this grain;
2.	There must always be a sufficient supply available to everyone everywhere.
3.	Storage facilities large enough for the needs of eastern consumers and western producers must be provided.
4.	It is recognized that water transportation is the cheapest of all but, unfortunately, it is of a seasonal nature; consequently, it would be appropriate to decentralize storage facilities.
5.	It is to be expected that grain consumption will increase by 50 per cent before 1975.
Yet, in 1960, it totalled 400 million bushels, 241 million of which had been produced in eastern Canada and the rest in the prairies. Generally speaking, pork and other meat producers buy 35 per cent of the feed grain they use; the other two thirds are produced on their own farms.
6.	Price fluctuation in various locations and at different times obviously constitutes a great impediment to producers. It is very important and fundamental to correct such a situation.
This policy is essential to stabilize the prices of grain and assist farmers.
In addition, the hon. member who spoke before me said that the price of feed grain rises when winter or the slack season arrives.
That is one of the reasons why a national emergency policy should be developed as soon as possible in order to remedy that situation and enable eastern producers to increase their net income without affecting western farmers.
We are a little pessimistic because the government seems to be marking time and not willing to do anything. Yet, to date, the minister has received several delegations, all kinds of eastern farmers organizations, which urged him to take action before it is too late.
Canadian tobacco growers and particularly Quebec growers are concerned at the present time because of the way they are treated by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh).
Indeed, the minister of national health allocated a tremendous amount of money to
Eastern Agricultural Assistance fight cancer and also published a pamphlet against the use of tobacco. To date, nothing proves that tobacco is the cause of cancer. Nothing was proven on that matter and scientists are at a variance. I wonder why the minister of national health wants to destroy that important sector of our economy, the production of cigarette tobacco.
I know that other government members also share my opinion. Tobacco growers are really concerned over the actions of the minister of national health and I am sending the Minister of Agriculture an s.o.s., asking him to make us aware of his future policy with a view to giving assistance to Canadian tobacco growers.
Tobacco sales have decreased noticeably following the bad publicity made by the minister of health, and I ask the Minister of Agriculture whether he approves the statements and the amounts of money voted by the department of health in order to fight smoking.
Growers are worried, and rightly so, and surely the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) is concerned also, since in 1962 tobacco sales brought in the tidy amount of about $178 million in taxes.
That is why I ask the Minister of Agriculture whether he intends to grant special votes or subsidies in order to help tobacco growers whose production represents an important factor of the Canadian economy.
I hope that the minister will give the house details which will reassure tobacco growers.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate because this party is seriously concerned with the question of rural life, the development of the family farm and all aspects of rural reconstruction; second, sir, because I am an old peasant farmer myself-I have lived off the land and on the land all my life and I am one of those who have always had their feet on the ground. The amendment reads:
That all the words after "That" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets the continuing failure of the government to take effective action with regard to the pressing agricultural problems of eastern Canada".
Personally, Mr. Speaker, I think the amendment is in too negative terms. What are the pressing agricultural problems of eastern Canada? They are not spelled out. Surely the whole field of agriculture in eastern Canada is not suffering from particular problems. Then, does this amendment mean that the official opposition are quite satisfied with the farm circumstances that exist in western Canada? I am really disappointed, in view of the

Eastern Agricultural Assistance agricultural talent that is to be found in the official opposition, that the amendment was not placed on a more constructive basis.
Before proceeding, Mr. Speaker, I do want to say that I give the former minister of agriculture full credit for his influence in securing the passage of the Farm Credit Corporation Act. It has been an excellent piece of legislation, but it is one of the pieces of legislation that, as the result of experience, needs improving. I give him full credit for the introduction of the ARDA program. The only thing that we want to see is some action in this respect in every province in Canada. And I give him full credit for publicly supporting the policy of wheat sales to China. At the time, leading members who are now on the government side were timidly trying to criticize this policy, but when they found what the public reaction was, they beat a hasty retreat.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Not the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson).

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: No. I give the hon. member for Red Deer full credit; he is positively opposed in principle to selling a bushel of wheat to those behind the iron curtain, and he stands fast on that position, regardless of what the farmers of his constituency think.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: A complete misrepresentation.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: I think I heard the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) chirping up; I think he said I was misrepresenting the hon. member for Red Deer. I will resume my seat, Mr. Speaker, and give the hon. member an opportunity to explain what I misrepresented.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: I would just remark, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) rose, I believe it was on Friday, and made his position very clear on this matter, on which the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) is possibly voicing his own opinions.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I missed something that the hon. member for Red Deer said recently, I must say now that I may be wrong-

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: You are not wrong, Bert.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
-but the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) informs me that the hon. member for Red Deer reiterated his stand in principle against the sale of wheat to countries behind the iron curtain. Anyway we did get things lined up a bit.
I listened to the speech made by the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Mullally) and I want to congratulate him on making a constructive

speech. He did not profess that there were no problems in agriculture. He recognized there were problems in eastern agriculture and in other sections of the country and was quite frank about it. As far as his speech is concerned, the implicit almost became the explicit when he was dealing with the need for action to improve these circumstances. However, I give him full credit for making a constructive speech under most difficult circumstances, seeing that he sits on the government side of the house.
We have a most unusual situation with respect to the two cabinet ministers whose duties are directly related to agriculture. We have the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), who announced at the foundation meeting- I do not know whether it was the foundation meeting or the foundering meeting-of the exchange of ideas organization that he is a socialist. Mind you, he was careful to say that he was not a parlour or a beer parlour socialist; he said he was a thinking socialist. He is now a director of an organization which I shall call the fraternity for the intellectually elite of Canada. So we have one announced socialist in the cabinet whose duties are directly related to agriculture. On the other side we have the ultimate in free enterprise in Canada. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) is the only person I have met in my experience in Canada who has publicly announced that his family believes in the principles of free enterprise after the resurrection. I must say I like the Minister of Agriculture and admire his frankness and honesty. Do you know what I have done to recognize that fact and to pay tribute to him, Mr. Speaker? I have just instructed the people on my ranch to rename our latest Hereford bull "Harry".

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Why?

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Hon. members ask me why. I will tell them why-because he is a great free enterpriser and a most successful salesman.
This is the dilemma I am in, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure many opposition members are too. I am not sure which of these policies is going to prevail, that of the socialist half of the agriculture team or that of the ultimate in free enterprise half. Therefore I am not certain in which direction this team is going. We have been quite conscious of the fact that in recent months there has been a bit of a tug of war, and I think it is around the basic philosophy of life which each of these gentlemen professes.
Going from the philosophical to the serious, shall I say, I want to say I fully support the plea put forward this afternoon by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) for

greater use of the agriculture committee of this house. Agriculture is one of our great and important industries in Canada, a way of life, shall 1 say, and the agriculture committee is not used to the extent it should be to obtain information. I am not one who suggests that there is an overnight solution to all these problems. I have had a bit of practical experience in life and come from a family which has a record in that respect, and has lived under pioneer conditions. We were so pioneer and so deficient in livestock that as far as I have been able to discover to date my family was the only family which owned a travelling rooster, which it used to ship up and down the Arrow lakes in a crate on a steamer. I just give that illustration to indicate that I have been closely associated with pioneer conditions. I believe hon. members of this house can learn a great deal by providing every possible opportunity-

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Is this a cock and bull story?

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member does not realize that it is a member of the opposition who is speaking.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: I guess it is only a bull story then.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
We are not using the brains and experience of persons connected with farm organizations of this country of all types. We should have a systematic exploration on, shall I say, a commodity and a regional, geographical basis of all the problems relating to farmers, which vary from province to province and make it more difficult for one set of legislation to cover all circumstances. That is a fact which we recognize, but I would urge the minister to give consideration to making greater use of our agriculture committee.
Another suggestion I want to make is for greater use of the committees of the Senate in this respect. If there is one thing the senators can do, something which I have urged for some time, it is committee work. We are not taking advantage of their opportunity to do this kind of work without, shall I say, the political atmosphere which surrounds members of this chamber on occasion when facing an election in the near future. The Senators can approach the matter in a more objective way. They are freed from those day to day concerns about re-election and so on. I have often thought that we could use committees of the Senate to study matters instead of appointing royal commissions, as we do in many cases and at great expense. There have been some good committees in the Senate. There was an excellent committee on narcotics. There was an excellent
Eastern Agricultural Assistance committee on manpower in Canada which made an excellent report.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: And on land use.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Yes; my leader mentions land use and I was just coming to that. This is a committee which has sat for several years and which has heard the opinions of responsible organizations across the country, accumulating a great deal of worth-while information which has not been made use of today.
To indicate this, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote from an editorial in the Western Producer of April 23, 1964:
In 1958 the committee proposed that the federal and provincial departments of agriculture speed up their soil surveys; that a systematic land use survey should be carried out across Canada; that further studies be made of drainage, erosion and irrigation problems.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, what has been done in that regard? In that connection I would ask the Minister of Agriculture what particular interest he has taken in land use problems relating to the Columbia river treaty. The national farmers' union of Canada has been very interested in and expressed their opinions on this matter. I believe this is a subject in which the federal and provincial departments of agriculture should have cooperated, and made a most exhaustive study of the land use possibilities of the whole basin.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: On a point of order.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: I can see I have got his dander up.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: I am just wondering whether this debate is to be allowed to develop into a debate on agriculture right across Canada. I had intended to speak on agriculture, but I suddenly realized this debate is limited to eastern agriculture, and therefore I refrained. If the hon. member intends to enter upon a general discussion of agriculture I think all members of the house should have the same opportunity.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
In reply to the hon. member for Fraser Valley, let me say I am speaking about eastern agriculture but using a western agricultural situation to illustrate my point.
The national farmers' union has been most concerned about this matter. They produced a brief some 10 pages long in which they pointed out the necessity for ensuring that supplies of water on the prairies from the Columbia are available in the future.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
I wonder if we might have a ruling before the hon. member proceeds further.

Eastern Agricultural Assistance

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Is this debate to be allowed to develop into a discussion of agriculture on a nation-wide basis?

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: It seems to me that the hon. member for Kootenay West is referring to agriculture generally, and maybe I could invite him to turn his thoughts eastward.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
I must explain that members of this party find it very difficult to divide the agriculturists of Canada into two. It is difficult to divide the philosophy behind the proper use of land and water into two parts. There are certain aspects of the problems of eastern agriculture which are common to all agriculturists in Canada and it is in that sense I am stepping over the boundary west of Winnipeg.
Anyway, they have gone into this question thoroughly, and I am wondering whether in view of the concern expressed by the national farmers union of Canada, an organization which has, of course, locals in Ontario, the minister has given serious consideration to this subject with a view to making certain that everything is done to having these resources properly surveyed, so that plans can be made for their future use.
So as not to further annoy the hon. member for Fraser Valley who is muttering behind me-

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext: The hon. member for Fraser Valley wants to speak on eastern agriculture; don't forget that.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
As usual, he will be behind me. Now I will go on with this editorial in the Western Producer, because I think more use could be made of these committees.
In 1959, the committee asked that the federal and provincial agriculture departments, together with universities and agricultural colleges, coordinate their farm research programs; that extension services should be expanded, with special attention being given to "farm management" for the alleviation of problems of the small uneconomic farm unit; that vocational and technical training programs be executed in rural areas; that authorities consider a program to give more resettlement assistance to any farmer on a small uneconomic farm wishing to move to another area of employment.
I should like the minister when he replies to inform the house what is being done to give effect to this recommendation of the Senate committee on land use which was made after listening to a good number of well presented briefs.
The article continues:
In 1961, the committee recommended that financial aid be given to farmers on submarginal lands in appropriate areas "to encourage reforestation of presently cultivated farm lands"; that surveys

be speeded up on urban expansion so as to bring about more orderly development of metropolitan areas; and that the committee sponsor special studies of rural taxation, land use for future recreational needs, river and lake pollution, and loss of good farm lands to "urban sprawl".
This is a very serious problem in eastern Canada. I presume this recommendation laid the foundation for the ARDA program, and I should also like the minister to tell the house when he replies what is being done by his department to give effect to this particular recommendation of the land use committee of the Senate.
I do not intend to pursue this editorial further. What I wish to emphasize is this: Here we have an agricultural committee of the House of Commons which is not used to the extent to which it could be used to assist agriculture in general as well as the government in power. In addition, we have a land use committee in the Senate which has been doing good work for two or three years, yet whose studies and recommendations have, on the whole, not been applied by the government of the day.
I was very glad to note recently the establishment of the agricultural economics research council of Canada. If the minister had any part in this, I give him full credit for it; I understand the organization will exist partially, at least, on federal and provincial grants. I think its objectives are very well stated. These are objectives which could very well be adopted by the agriculture committee of the House of Commons as well as by the corresponding committee in the other place. A document on this subject which I have before me contains a brief statement of the purpose and nature of each of four projects. It reads as follows:
The first project will be a study of the relationship between Canadian agricultural policy and what is generally referred to as the farm problem. The purpose of the study is to analyse the objective of past and present farm policies and relates them to the programs which have been implemented to achieve these objectives.
The second project will be an economic analysis of the feed grain freight assistance policy. The study will attempt to determine where the freight subsidies actually go.
The third project is a study of the capital supply for Canadian agriculture.
This is a most necessary study.
The fourth study is designed to study the place of agriculture in the national economy-
The board also announced that all research carried out by the council will be published and made available to the public.
I would hope that members of this house can get information about the work done by this research council and that we shall have the opportunity to co-operate with these important activities both in the committee of this house and in the other place. I also suggest

that if we are to find solutions to the agricultural problems not only of eastern Canada but of the whole of Canada there must be more co-operation between federal and provincial governments. We have to secure the co-operation of the farmers organizations and more participation on the part of farmers organizations in the development of studies and the provision of information. I must say that as far as farming is concerned, very often someone who is unsung, in some backwoods district, one might say, comes forward with an idea which is eventually accepted by the majority. We should cultivate the soil of experience and knowledge which are found among the farmers of this country. I think we should make better use of the Agricultural Institute of Canada. I happen to be a charter member of that organization and I am very interested in its activities. In passing I might say to the minister that I think the salaries paid to agriculturists in Canada are very much out of line with those paid to other scientific and professional workers and they should receive some further consideration.
Then we must achieve the closest possible co-operation between people and governments. I believe in the principle of co-operation and participation. I should not say "I do": We all do in this party. This is the way in which democratic policies evolve. People like to feel they are consulted-that they are wanted- that they are part of a team. This is necessary if we are to develop an agricultural policy in this country. In addition, we must have cooperation with the press.
I want to say a few words about the agricultural press of Canada. Anyone who has been a reader of the agricultural press of Canada for over 50 years, as I have, knows that it is the most responsible section of the press in this country. I want to pay tribute to the work they have done for agriculture. I want to pay tribute to the Family Herald for the excellent articles it prints with respect to water resources and land use problems, its editorials concerning the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) and so on. I have enjoyed every one of them. I pay tribute also to the Western Producer and the press of the co-operative organizations.
This is not a press that prints only the spectacular or the thing that catches the eye. To many people I suppose this type of periodical is dull reading. For instance, a member of this house can get up and make a most constructive and well informed speech on the principles of conservation or something relating to agriculture, and you will find that most of the press is not very interested, but if one gets up in the house and
Eastern Agricultural Assistance abuses the minister, instead of complimenting him like I have this evening, it is headline news.
I refer also to Country Life published in British Columbia, and the multitude of other agricultural periodicals. I am sure if the government made a particular effort to get the co-operation of the agricultural press behind a defined policy and program they would get it without a shadow of a doubt. If we can get the co-operation I have been suggesting, and benefit from the experience and knowledge found abundantly among many people in this country, we will solve the problems of eastern agriculture and western agriculture in the near future, instead of having to repeat year after year in the house the fact that there are certain problems which remain unsolved because we have not developed the co-operation to meet them effectively. That is all I have to say, Mr. Speaker.

maintopic: LACK OF ACTION TO ASSIST EASTERN AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to point out, at the outset of my remarks which I shall make as brief as possible, that I am primarily speaking in my capacity as member for a Quebec constituency which is partly rural and partly industrialized; that kind of mixture back home accounts for the fact that our farm problem is probably more acute.
This afternoon and tonight, I heard various excellent speeches on agriculture. Some I have appreciated more than others. I have also heard some quite caustic criticisms from across, and I hope that I will not commit such a mistake. I quite agree that it is the duty of the opposition to offer criticism, but when we reach a point where former governments are criticized and comparisons are made with this one and that one, it seems to me there are certain limits which should not be exceeded.
I do not necessarily need to know if the previous government, or those preceding it, should have done more or less, because I am only concerned with finding a solution to the existing farm problem. Eastern Canada is obviously in need of assistance and it is not so much a matter of recalling the saddest phases perhaps in the farm history of eastern Canada as of trying to bring a little sunshine to clouded areas. And when I say sunshine, I am using the word in its literal as well as its figurative sense.
Many topics have been discussed today, but we know that the eastern climate is in no way to be compared with the western climate, which does make a difference as far as agriculture is concerned. Even if we had the most

Eastern Agricultural Assistance intelligent minister to look specifically after eastern agriculture, I do not think he could pull the strings which would give us the required weather when and where we need it. Those are factors that must be taken into consideration, but which seem to be criticized from certain sides. I am thinking, among others, of an hon. member I do not need to mention by name and who is very strong on farm matters. He should bring a few more new ideas instead of referring to the same old things, because he has run out of subjects of criticism. If he had done that at the time he held the required post-that is the only indication I shall give-perhaps we would have less to do now.
A while ago, it seems that the merits of the minister who is responsible today for the administration of ARDA were being discussed and, to a certain extent, even questioned. The so-called ARDA legislation is a program which, personally, I hold in high respect and the same goes for the people in my riding, the farmers themselves and those who go in for part-time farming or are involved in mining research of some kind.
In fact, we have been told that ARDA itself will be revised. In certain quarters, it was said that the responsible minister might not have the time to look after forestry. Be that as it may, the fact remains that in a riding such as mine and in other neighbouring counties, agriculture has just as many problems as forestry. Indeed, problems are often related in both fields. As far as I am concerned, I am quite happy that both questions should come under the same department. I am sure that the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), who is also responsible for ARDA, will know how to handle the situation.
It is a pleasure for me to congratulate hon. members opposite for having set up ARDA, because when somebody does something worth while, I like to say it.
What is the present status of ARDA? Before coming here, I inquired several times of agronomists, but the situation is so vague that no one seems to know what benefits we derive from the program. Explanations were given today and as a television writer who is well known in the Quebec area once said: It is not over. Other explanations and instructions will be forthcoming but, what is most important, I can promise you some action, whether hon. members opposite like it or not. It will not be a vision, a castle in the air. It is not a house of cards that the new minister wishes to build; he wants something more solid and it seems to me that one cannot help admire the energetic efforts he has made and is still making so as to obtain beneficial results with his department. That is why he 
wants to work hard and will draw his inspiration, I am sure of that, as he has done in the past, from the speeches made on both sides of the house, at least from the speeches made in French, because it would be very hard to find something in a wasteland of ideas, and unfortunately that is the main dish we have been served too often.
I was pleased to note this afternoon that sincere and serious people in the various parties really made it their duty to express to the house their worries and those of their constituents about agriculture.
To come back to ARDA, I am happy that at this very moment, the minister responsible for the administration of that act is in Manitoba. When he comes back to the house in the next few days, he will have visited the prairie provinces, the eastern provinces, the maritime provinces and also the provinces next to British Columbia.
When he meets the premiers of those provinces and discusses farm problems with them he will see in which way we may, not so much establish ARDA, because that has been already done, but improve this legislation and make it become more helpful than we could expect until now.
At this point I associate myself with the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Laver-diere), who represents the riding next to mine, who said on May 7 last, as we may find on page 3046 of Hansard:
For the good of the country, of confederation and of agriculture also, there must be an understanding between eastern and western Canada-
It is not only in the international field that a meeting is needed between east and west.
One region can help the other and each can complete the other, especially in the production of feed grain which is so urgently needed for our eastern cattle.
He had previously quoted many statistics which are found on pages 3045 and 3046 of the official record. I would rather let you read them for yourself, Mr. Speaker, than repeat what has already been said. Anybody who wants to play about with statistics, handles them as a knife with two sharp edges so that he sometimes cuts himself with the wrong edge. It becomes somewhat boring in the end perpetually to be quoting figures. With regard to the problem now under discussion and which concerns all provinces, including Quebec and the maritimes, it would be needless, I think, to quote so many statistics. It is true that our farmers' income is surely not comparable to the income of western farmers. It is also true that the previous governments-I am not saying "government"-seemed to be particularly concerned

with the western farmers, who have taken a lead of which I am not envious. I can understand their enhancing their own business.
That is why today, we must unite our efforts, the efforts of conscientious members on both sides of the house who wish to bring something to eastern farmers who, I think, were too often done wrong, did not get enough assistance and got bogged down. But the fault does not necessarily rest with the federal Department of Agriculture because in every province, there is also a provincial department of agriculture which may be even more directly responsible because they are directly in the area.
In the province of Quebec, it is clear that we had many farming problems at the provincial level.
Whatever leeway there was, an effort is being made now to make it up. It is precisely through that co-operation and following that profitable visit of the present minister, responsible for the new start in ARDA, that we shall finally have more concrete solutions and take more direct steps to assist the farmers.
Help can be given in so many fields.
Another interesting feature of ARDA is that it is not exactly centred only on our farmers. As I said earlier, it can be applied to mines, forestry and many other things, fisheries, everything that can be economic, even industry.
That is why, first of all, work is now being done in my riding as well as in my province, as in the other provinces of eastern Canada, to collect data and complete basic work, for it would be useless to go ahead with the first plan that comes to mind. That was done already, not long ago, and we saw the result. It is better somewhat to delay things in order to arrive at more far reaching and reliable solutions.
Of course several hon. members here would be able to discuss farm problems more interestingly than I can, because I never had the opportunity of looking much into agricultural problems all over Canada, not even in my own riding. But we have seen by now that our farmers had to have some income besides the revenue from their land, because they had trouble in getting along, in finding a decent income enabling them to live and educate their children and so on.
I admit all that, but we must also recognize for instance, that there could have been a somewhat closer supervision, because I think that in the east, and more particularly in Quebec, as hon. members from Quebec are more interested in this matter than others, our farmers may be more inclined to quicker

Eastern Agricultural Assistance mechanization so that the farms might yield quicker profit, instead of going about it more gradually.
Horses have been abandoned and, today, we have to use tractors, pick-ups and station-wagons on a farm which yields very little, because of unfavourable weather, and which cannot produce enough to ensure a steady income and especially some profit. What is the result? In a constituency like mine great difficulties have been experienced. For instance, a poultry-farmer has to work in the bush in order to make ends meet and pay for his big tractor, while he should have bought a smaller one. He is therefore obliged, during the winter months, to go and work in the state of Maine, or he has to serve on the ships of the Department of Transport. In brief, he tries to find a way to earn some money.
With the implementation of the ARDA program, a better balanced and better thought out program, with a more equitable redistribution of the tillable lands at home, I believe it would be appropriate for the serious farmer to take advantage of the appropriate help which will be offered to him by the Department of Agriculture at the federal as well as the provincial level. Then the farmer could stay on his farm and, in that way, we will not only help him but also the class of forest workers who face a yearly invasion of their field of endeavour by these part-time lumbermen, farmers by profession, who, in order to survive, are compelled to practise several other trades. Thus we would even fight unemployment if a well thought out program were put to work adequately.
That is why, in order not to waste the time of the house, I want to express again all the confidence I have in the present Minister of Agriculture and congratulate him for the work he has done.
I would like things to go faster and the eastern farmer would be delighted.
With regard to supplying feed grain to the eastern farmer, I noticed last year, like all the other members, that the Department of Agriculture had taken a big step forward. When the shipping season opened, it paid for the transportation right away to fill our grain elevators, especially to help our farmers.
Personally, I felt that that was sound but our farmers did not get as much as they would have hoped, even if prices did go up a little.
Who made the profits? I suspect that certain big companies made profits and are still making some. However, co-operatives are

Eastern Agricultural Assistance having difficulties because the price of pork has dropped while that of feed grain is excessive.
I wonder what would have happened if, for instance, the government had not filled the grain elevators? Perhaps the situation would be even worse. Of course, that is not enough but at least we got off on the right foot.
There has been a lot of talk about the effect of the price of feed grain on the dairy industry. We have within our ranks experts who can explain the situation much more clearly than I could and some of them will explain the statistics and set straight the facts which have been somewhat altered, I might say, by some members of the opposition. Figures will be given and explanations provided. Other explanations may not deal with statistics but they will be useful just the same.
In short, we surely have a lot to do yet, but it is certainly not through criticism that we will accomplish anything. As far as I am concerned, when the opportunity arises, it will always be a pleasure to express the grievances of my constituents because they do not always have the time to come to Ottawa to meet the minister and lay their problems before him. Besides, that is what I was asked to do.
But for the time being I know that at home -and when I say at home I mean, of course, in my constituency of Montmagny-L'Islet- even if we are hoping for a more vital and more specific solution, we realize that efforts are being made along those lines.
I am positive that the Minister of Forestry and the officials of ARDA are doing a marvellous job and that we will surely have better days and a sounder policy, because it will be a clearer policy, stemming from on the spot study. Instead of throwing up a big balloon to float everywhere, we will anchor it so as to derive the greatest possible benefits therefrom.
I leave you with that note of confidence in the present administration, but I will commend the government when the situation has improved, while hoping it will not deteriorate. I am looking forward to a greater improvement as soon as possible and so, I am urging the ministers concerned to continue their efforts with the help of qualified officials of the department.
I also say to our hon. friends opposite, no matter to what party they belong, that when they make proper suggestions, when they offer something acceptable, something constructive and positive, instead of only negative suggestions, then we will be happy to give them our co-operation. I see that the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pi-

geon) now has a smile on his face. When he has good suggestions, it will give me pleasure to encourage him and to support him.
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry I took more time than I intended to, but it is in that spirit of co-operation with the hon. members of the opposition that I did so and, in return, I am asking for their co-operation. When they will actually give us their co-operation, that will be the day we will succeed in solving, as quickly as possible and in the most adequate way, the problem which is affecting everyone of us in eastern Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have heard some excellent debating this evening and, as usual, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) lit up the chamber with his sense of humour. Coming from the same city as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) I say with a lot of respect that when the hon. member for Kootenay West said he was going to call his prize white faced bull Harry, that is quite a compliment, because the minister will agree with me that some of the best Hereford stock is bred in the province of Alberta. I might not have gone quite that far myself, but it is still a compliment to the minister.
I was most interested in hearing the hon. member for Kootenay West discussing how the division of agriculture had been made, and in fact the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) was wondering how we people from western Canada might discuss agriculture on this amendment. I had better answer that right now. It seems to me we should have one department of agriculture and one minister of agriculture. Then we might have a healthy agricultural colony across the country because, when the wheat farmers of western Canada are doing well, they will not get into severe competition with eastern farmers who raise cattle and hogs and produce other agricultural commodities.
When one speaks critically he should also have something constructive to offer. I think the minister is a practical man, even if he believes in free enterprise after resurrection, as the hon. member for Kootenay West said this evening; but it seems strange to me that, even with one of the best contracts for grain ever made with Russia-a contract which was first made by the former government and then developed by this government-we were unable to supply the full quantities needed, or at least were unable to say to the Russian people that we could supply the full demand.
Make no mistake about it, Mr. Speaker, we had the supply of grain in western Canada. We had one of the finest wheat crops

ever, and if that grain could have been moved to the facilities at the ports, and from the ports to Russia, then probably the United States would never have signed its wheat sale agreement with Russia.
Therefore I say to the minister as I said a year ago, and as I said to the former government, some serious thought should be given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), working in conjunction with one minister of agriculture-

We have the demand and the supply, but we as a country boast too much about the things we have, while forgetting to put our handling facilities in shape, our railroads, our terminal elevators, and relations between management and labour, so that we can meet the demand.
Coming from the same city as the Minister of Agriculture, where he is well recognized because he was the former mayor, I say to him he has a chance to make a name for himself, if he will discuss this problem with the Minister of Trade and Commerce and have a serious discussion with the railroads. I have heard senior members of the house tell how grain supplies used to be discussed for weeks on end in this chamber. That is no longer a subject for debate because the farmers are getting the big crops on the prairies and we have the contracts to sell the grain. maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST FRENCH CANADIAN ARMY OFFICERS
NATIONAL DEFENCE-ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST FRENCH CANADIAN ARMY OFFICERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 7 last I asked the Minister of National Defence a question regarding the discrimination against French Canadians in the Kingston military college and I quote:
Is it the minister's intention to prescribe an inquiry, following the statement made by Mr. Arstae Lauziere, professor at the military college in Kingston to the effect that there is at the present time a certain discrimination against the French Canadians, as far as their promotion within the Canadian army is concerned?
Mr. Speaker, having received no answer, I asked that that question be taken up later.
I think it would be important for the government to set up as soon as possible a commission, perhaps a royal commission, on the Canadian army, with a limited period of time, in order to establish whether the quite serious charges made by the professor at the Kingston military college are true.
Le Devoir of May 12 last reproduced the statement of a senior army officer that French Canadians are not discriminated against in the army. Major General Worthington stated:
A French Canadian soldier who speaks English has the same promotion opportunities as anybody else.
We often hear such statements in Englishspeaking military quarters and, to begin with, they are quite true. Promotions are based on seniority and merit, and that simple rule applies down to intermediate ranks.
However, so that this statement may apply adequately to the problem, a few implications have to be added which show that, if there is no discrimination, there is surely some injustice.
I should like to ask the minister-one of the two ministers of national defence is probably here this evening, even if I do not see either of them now-why is military instruction only given in English and not in both languages. Second, why is only one language used as far as work, correspondence and orders are concerned? Third, the soldier must serve wherever he is sent, with all the invitations that implies to put his own language aside, since he finds himself in a


unilingual environment. I am of the opinion that the French speaking soldier should be on the same footing as the English speaking soldier. Fourth, a member of the armed forces who insists on remaining in the province of Quebec to ensure a French education for his children is considered a trouble-maker and his promotion is affected.
Mr. Speaker, I think there is some uneasiness and we are aware of it as a result of the great number of letters which we on this side of the house are receiving. This uneasiness among French Canadians is experienced in the three services. Of course, there is the royal 22nd regiment, which is mostly made up of French Canadians, but I wonder whether the Minister of National Defence could not establish other French speaking regiments or else some regiments half of which would be made up of French speaking and the other half of English speaking servicemen.
I feel it is not enough that the Laurendeau-Dunton commission will examine behind closed doors members of the armed forces who will express such a wish. In my opinion, another investigation should be conducted so as to know exactly what is going on in the armed services and to let the public know.
Serious doubts still exist in the public mind, and I hope that the Minister of National Defence, in the interest of national unity, will act as soon as possible in order to know whether or not there is discrimination against French Canadian servicemen.
