subtopic: SAINT JOHN, N.B.   TRANSFER OF MANUFACTURING FIRM TO MONTREAL
SAINT JOHN, N.B.   TRANSFER OF MANUFACTURING FIRM TO MONTREAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday I asked a question of the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) in the absence of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), so I am delighted that it is the Minister of Transport who is fulfilling all the responsibilities this evening. I asked:
In view of the closing of the national manufacturing concern of McAvity's in Saint John and its transfer to Montreal with all its facilities, resulting in a loss of more than 400 jobs, will the Atlantic development board immediately investigate and offer every assistance in this matter?
This question was ruled out of order by Your Honour, I suppose because of the lack of urgency. I suggest that this matter is very urgent because meetings are now being held in Saint John between the provincial government, civic officials and bodies, and company officers in an effort to save and possibly retain this industry, and failing this to consider possible alternatives for the plant and men. Therefore it is imperative, in my opinion, that the federal government be represented at these discussions.
This shutdown in Saint John has been one of the most serious blows which we have experienced for some time in this community. The hon. member for Charlotte has some business interests in the city and I think he will agree that this has been one of the toughest blows it has experienced in many years. Over 400 skilled men without pension are to be thrown on to the already meagre labour market. There will be little opportunity for them to relocate in Montreal. Though some may find it possible to obtain work in other industries, the great bulk of these men will have serious readjustment problems. I recognize that this is primarily a matter for the provincial government, and in all fairness I should say that they are taking an interest and are the ones who have arranged this meeting. However, at the same time the present Robichaud government has taken considerable credit for new industry in the province and have given rise to fantastic stories about great job opportunities for everyone. This closing down of a long established family industry will certainly be a lesson to them and they will think twice about making lavish claims in the future.
There is another ironic twist to this, in that we have just made plans for the completion of a large newsprint industry in the city which was arranged by the previous Flemming government of New Brunswick. It is presently under construction and will be ready for operation in ten months. But as
25, 1964	3577
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion optimistic as this is, it will not fill the hole left in the labour market by the McAvity closing.
Similarly, announcements were made in the local papers which appeared in the Toronto newspapers last Saturday that Du Pont will open a new industry there. This is the first to be located by that company in the Atlantic provinces. This is good news, but the truth is that the Du Pont mill will employ only about 12 men for their polyethylene processing.
I suggest that the Atlantic development board immediately send representatives to sit in at the Saint John meetings to obtain first hand information as to the reason this industry can no longer continue. They should examine the economics. Is it the old bogey of geography? Is it a case of freight rate disadvantages, or are there other hidden reasons? What is the responsibility of the internationally owned and controlled Crane Company who purchased McAvity four years ago and is now for some strange reason closing out their Saint John operation in favour of Montreal? It seems that everything is going to Montreal. It may be that the area development agency of the Department of Industry should be involved, and if it is felt by the minister that this would be better, it is all right with me. We are spending thousands of dollars to find out how to locate new secondary manufacturing in the maritimes. We are sending representatives all over the world-I know that some of the permanent officials of the Atlantic development board are presently in Scotland-to study methods which have been successful in other countries which have had this problem. Yet here at our own doorstep, and at the very moment these commendable efforts are being accelerated, this industry, long established and at one time the largest foundry in Canada, is shutting down. Therefore, I call on the minister to say that the federal government will send representatives to these conferences and enthusiastically assist in finding a solution to this problem, one which goes to the very core of our regional geographic disabilities in the maritimes.
I see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), with his great interest in the maritime provinces, is following closely, and this is one time when he has to rise to the occasion and show some sincere helpfulness in this respect.
